speakerposition: subtopic
Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There are 11 report stage motions on today's notice paper in amendment to Bill C-98, an act authorizing agreements between the Government of Canada and the provinces to provide for protection for the income of producers of agricultural products and to enable the Government of Canada to take additional measures for that purpose.
Motions Nos. 1, 2 and 3, standing in the name of the hon. member for Mackenzie, caused the Chair to examine at length the procedural acceptability of the motions. But, after careful reflection, I have decided to give the benefit of the doubt to the member.
Motions Nos. 1, 2 and 3 will be grouped for debate and a vote on motion No. 1 will apply to motions Nos. 2 and 3.
Motion No. 4, standing in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, motion No. 5, standing in the name of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, and motions Nos. 6, 7, 8 and 9 standing in the name of the hon. member for Algoma, are all procedurally acceptable. They will be debated and voted on separately.
Motion No. 10, standing in the name of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, and motion No. 11 standing in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, both deal with reports to Parliament, more specifically review of act. Both motions are in order. They will be grouped for debate and an affirmative vote on motion No. 10 obviates the need for a vote on motion No. 11. A negative vote on motion No. 10 will require the question being put on motion No. 11.
I will now propose motions Nos. 1, 2 and 3 to the House.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-98 be amended in Clause 4 by striking out line 37 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"program provided the maximum account built up by any one producer does not exceed $100,000 in 1991 dollars;".
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-98 be amended in Clause 4 by striking out line 38 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"(b) a gross revenue insurance program provided maximum payments to anyone producer do not exceed $ 100,000 per annum in 1991 dollars;".
Motion No. 3
That Bill C-98 be amended in Clause 4 by striking out line 39 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
March 21, 1991

Government Orders
"(c) a revenue insurance program provided maximum payments to any one producer do not exceed $100,000 per annum in 1991 dollars; and".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the basic reasoning behind these particular amendments is one of permitting Parliament to exert its normal influences. This particular piece of legislation is one of the most wide open chunks of parliamentary business that I have seen in my 11 years in the House. There is no recourse to the normal role of parliamentarians to set limits to the amount of money being expended, to have any control over expenditures, which is one of the basic roles that Parliament plays in our system, or is supposed to play in our system.
Because we are representing taxpayers in this bill, as well as farmers, I felt that it was incumbent upon us in the House to decide what the maximum limits, liabilities if you will, to the public purse should be with some clarity. I have proposed that the maximum limits of liability from the public purse in each of the programs be set at $100,000. The GRIP program, which is motion No. 2, is a gross revenue insurance program. The maximum liability from the public purse, from the GRIP payment fund would be $100,000 per producer.
What does that mean? By my admittedly rough calculations, but all of the calculations I hasten to add having to do with GRIP are rough, this would catch farmers in the open plains with farms where they are seeding above 5,000 acres. In the higher producing areas of the country, it would perhaps catch people over 4,000 acres of seeded crop. When we get into the heavy com producing part of the country, that acreage might be reduced to 1,500 or 1,800 acres as a rough guess.
At any rate, it cuts out very few people at the present time who would not extract the maximum possible payment on any particular year. The coming year is considered to be a year with a very large payment probability. Even under these expected high pay-outs, it would take a very large seeded acreage before the $100,000 ceiling would reduce the amount of payment under the price support part of this program.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, being very observant, that I did not propose to put any ceiling on the pay-outs under crop insurance. There is a very good reason for that.
Crop insurance is a more direct insurance program which insures against production at current market prices. There is no perceived rip-off of taxpayers' money, to use the kind of wording I am already hearing in my towns and villages, to maintain very large farms.
However, when taxpayers are putting up 42 and one-third per cent of their tax dollars into this maximum pay-out of $100,000 on an annual basis and an additional 25 per cent of their provincial tax dollars into this pay-out, they are starting to think that that is quite a lot of money to go to one farmer. Therefore, I think we should be putting some ceilings on it at this stage.
The numbers that I have already put on the record sound very high and very scary to most taxpayers who perhaps are not as well inculcated into farm economics and who probably do not realize that this is still unlikely to give a net income to most of those farmers, even so.
Once we get into the sizes of operation where this ceiling will apply, I think there can be a justifiable public policy reason for putting these ceilings in place. I do regret that the three proposals were put under one set of debating points, because the first one is considerably different than Motions Nos. 2 and 3. It would have been easier to debate the concept and the principle, had Motion No. 1 been separated from Motions Nos. 2 or 3.1 accept your ruling and your wisdom, Mr. Speaker, and will attempt to present the arguments in a series, even though some of the economic and accounting principles involved in Motion No. 1 are quite different from those in Motions Nos. 2 and 3.
Motion No. 3 places $100,000 a ceiling on the pay-out to be received by any one producer under those commodities now covered by the Agricultural Stabilization Act. That act did have some ceilings as did the old Western Grain Stabilization Act, which to a certain extent GRIP replaces.
The concept or idea of ceilings is certainly not new. The ceilings that are being placed here are very adequate. They will not offend very many people and will only trigger a reduction in a pay-out to a very minor

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
groups of individuals. I think it is the role of this Parliament and the role of parliamentarians to set some limits, even though they are not particularly stringent limits, on the expenditures of this and future governments and on the ability to sign federal-provincial agreements which have absolutely no upper limit on the public purse.
Therefore I put these forward for consideration in the Elouse. There is very little more to say on this issue. It does not assist in public policy, in economic policy, or in rural development for extended amounts of public money to be put into one particular economic group in rural areas.
It creates some economic problems, some economic disruptions, yes; but it also creates great social and political unrest when ordinary taxpayers, who are perhaps under current conditions sitting on an unemployment insurance cheque as their only source of income which is capped and cannot go above a certain limit, watch their farm neighbours reportedly getting pay-outs to address their particular economic difficulties which go even beyond $100,000 per year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments. I certainly understand the hon. member's well-taken points.
I want to remind this House and all hon. members that this legislation was developed in close collaboration with Canadian farmers. We relied on the grains and oilseeds safety net committee, a majority of whom were producers. That committee, in its report presented to ministers of agriculture last August, did not call for caps on farm size or for payments. In its report, the committee indicated that "GRIP participation is open to all economic units" and "there should be no maximum on payments from GRIP".
This view was echoed by other farm leaders who appeared before the agriculture standing committee. Mr. Terry Daynard, speaking on behalf of the Ontario Corn Producers Association, indicated his group's policy was to oppose caps. Mr. Owen Mcauley of Keystone Agricultural Producers indicated: "I know our organization is opposed to caps".
Farm leaders, quite apart from anything else, know that once caps are put on any program administrative problems are created, as large farmers are virtually forced to split their enterprise into smaller units to avoid the maximum set by the program.
We do not feel that these motions would enhance the legislation. It could create problems, as I have just indicated. Therefore the government is not prepared to accept these three amendments.

Mr. Speaker, the amendments put before the House today did not receive a lot of discussion in committee, although some farm groups did recommend that there be no cap. We believe there should be a review of the legislation within two years.
If we look at the government's program for interest assistance, it is providing for a maximum of interest-free support of $50,000. The western grain stabilization fund at the present time has a cap of $50,000 per year. There is a lot of uncertainties in this legislation as to exactly how it is going to work.
We in the House of Commons, and I am sure the provincial legislatures, feel rather outside the deals that are going on between the governments involved. This is part of the new executive federalism which has really replaced the parliamentary system in this country. Our ability actually to spell out what the GRIP program is going to be and what the NISA program is going to be is sharply circumscribed.
I can see problems with sharply circumscribing what those agreements can be. For instance, in the horticultural industry we are dealing with a high value crop per acre. This is all based on gross revenue not on the price of individual commodities, although that is a factor in what the gross revenue would be per acre. At the same time, when we are dealing with the NISA program, it is inconceivable that it will reach the cap until after the review takes place, if that review takes place as we have recommended in 1993.
If we are dealing with a legislation which is going to be reviewed in two years' time, the concept would be acceptable to our side of the House although the government has already indicated that it is not acceptable to it.
March 21, 1991

If there is any overriding situation in this whole thing, certainly for western fanners it is just not knowing what the limits are or what the premiums are. They received the estimates of premiums several days after the legislation was actually brought in. They really do not know what to do, whether to farm the program in order to maximize revenues or whether to go strictly on the market forces. The market signals of course are very limited as far as the price of commodities.
There was a report this morning by a forecasting group in the United States which projects a very marked increase in the number of acres being planted for grain crops in Canada. It associates this in some way with the implementation of the GRIP.
I think there are arguments on both sides. We certainly do not have any high value horticultural crops coming under NISA and GRIP at this stage because they have not been developed. They may be at a later stage, but we would hope the government would agree at a later stage in discussion of the bill today to accept an earlier review, rather that five years, in which case the cap of $100,000 as proposed probably would not cause any great hardship even to those high value crops such as the grains and oilseeds. In any event, this limit would increase the value, the pay-out or the benefit by 100 per cent from the existing western grain stabilization fund.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak to some of these amendments today to Bill C-98, the legislation that allows the government to enter into agreements on the GRIP and NISA programs.
One matter that concerns me a lot about this process was brought home to me when the parliamentary secretary talked about the consultation process, the producers being involved in the process which led to this program being developed and now this legislation in front of us to enter into these agreements.
The parliamentary secretary said that this consultation process had occurred. What he neglected to say was that the consultation process involved general discussions about the need for safety net and some specifics about how we should go about it.
Government Orders
However, the consultation process with the farm community not only since the program has been developed, but this legislation has been entered into in this Chamber, has been very poor. The consultation process with people who at this point on the farm are still very confused about what the GRIP and NISA programs mean to them is something that should be examined in much greater detail.
I am quite concerned that the confusion out there and the need for an immediate infusion of cash are driving individuals both in this Chamber and in the provincial legislatures to reach agreements more quickly than they should otherwise be prepared to enter into them. That is why I believe this amending process in the Chamber today is so very important.
This legislation simply allows for agreements to be entered into. The bill calls for an April 1 implementation date, April 1 being of course just the end of next week, April 1 being a very close deadline to be working with.
The provincial legislature of Saskatchewan is not in session to pass similar legislation allowing the province of Saskatchewan to enter into an agreement with the federal government on this program. The provincial legislature has said that it will not even begin sitting until the end of the first or the second week of April.
As a result, the mandate from the provincial legislature of the province of Saskatchewan to allow that government to enter into agreement with the federal government cannot even begin to take place until several days after the legislation is supposed to come into force.
The farm community is certainly desperately in need of cash. This is one reason why I stood last week and called for the application of the finance minister's $1.3 million budgeted for farmers in need to be applied immediately for spring seeding. That would bridge the gap and allow for better understanding and the creation of a stronger safety net program so that not only those of us in the House understood completely, but that the farm community, farm producers and individuals operating on farms throughout Saskatchewan, western Canada and elsewhere, would have an understanding of what this program meant to them and could assess it properly.
My biggest concern in all of this is that in the long term we may have a very deficient program. The provincial leader in Saskatchewan, Roy Romanow, has said that this might be the shortest long-term program in the history of agriculture programs. What he meant by that was that

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
farmers will be in it for the first couple of years to get the pay-outs that are predicted and will then withdraw from the program, leaving the program with a huge deficit and still no solution to the farm income crisis of producers.
The three amendments before us were put forward by my colleague from Mackenzie, a long-time New Democratic agriculture critic. He is someone who is respected throughout the agricultural community, particularly by producers in the province of Saskatchewan. The amendments try to put some reason to the carte blanche blank cheque legislation that is in front of us until such time as we can properly assess some of the long-term implications.
We cannot accept a blank cheque for the government simply to enter agreements with the provinces on legislation which may in fact over the long term completely alter the way in which agricultural support programs are delivered in Canada.
When we look at the pieces of that legislation that have to amend, we see that some of these deficiencies can be corrected in the short term. For example, putting a cap on the amounts of funds available in NISA, as this particular amendment proposes, prevents the government from doing in farming what it is already doing in banking, in business, and in running our economy, that is helping to reward those who already have a lot, the wealthy large farmers who are not part of the serious debt and income crisis on the prairies and allowing the government to match dollar for dollar farmers who are capable and able to put large amounts of money into the Net Income Stabilization Account.
By matching those dollars the government gives tremendous benefit to those who have the wealth and prevents those who do not have the wealth from getting into it. As we have heard in committee, in this House, and around the country, NISA does nothing to support the poorer farmers, the marginal farmers, the farmers who are in debt both to the banks and to the government's financial institutions. This bill does nothing to address that long-term debt problem. Therefore, if we can do anything at all to ensure that the discrimination in favour of the wealthy producers in this country can be held in check somewhat until we can address the debt
and income problems in the long term, we are accomplishing something. This blank cheque legislation allows for agreements of almost any kind, and is contrary to the development of long-term success of income stabilization on the prairies. I would remind the House that we have not seen those agreements.
I urge the government to accept these few amendments put forward by the hon. member for Mackenzie. I am pleased to hear that members of the opposition are prepared to accept these amendments. If the government can accept these amendments as well, we can achieve some small sense of fairness in a bill which does provide for quite a bit of unfairness if left to stand unchecked.
I will have other things to say on other amendments throughout the day. With that, I will provide the floor to other members.

Mr. Speaker, I want to give my support to the position put forward by my good colleague from Algoma. I will restrict my few remarks to the matter of caps.
Farmers are very responsible people. They expect us to be responsible people. While in the eyes of some people, caps may be construed as being discriminatory, we do have to exercise some caution and certainly exercise responsibility.
The safety net programs which we are embarking upon are something very new to us. They are new to the country and new to the producers. We are, in a sense, going through uncharted waters. All the more reason, in my mind, why we have to be super-responsible. That is why I, and the rest of us on this side, favour caps at least for this particular time, and want a thorough review of this legislation two years down the road.
We want to be responsible. We do not want to hurt anyone. We do not want to discriminate against anyone. We are up against something which is new and we do not know exactly how these things are going to develop. For example, arriving on my desk just this morning is a report from a group in the United States called the Wharton Economic Forecasting Association. It claims that wheat acreage in western Canada is going to jump over a
March 21, 1991

million acres this spring. I do not know whether it is going to be right or wrong.
This is one of the unknowns that we face. It combines two things; first, that we want to be responsible about this, and second, that we want to have a thorough review a couple of years down the road when we have the benefit of some experience and the benefit of some facts that may be not available to us now. I think it would be very, very prudent to go along with these caps, certainly on the NISA program. Prudence also demands that we place a cap on GRIP, at least for the next couple of years.
I simply want to put this on the record.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two or three very brief comments with respect to the amendments we have in front of the House.
Somebody mentioned the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I should point out that the act provides for coverage of 90 per cent of eligible income in the prairie region. In one sense, it provides a cap, but it is up to 90 per cent of the aggregate income in the prairie region. That has been adjusted, I believe, three times. It started out at 25 per cent, it went to 40 per cent and it is now at 60 per cent.
We came close to raising it to 90 per cent; $1,000 per farmer, $25,000 to $40,000 per farm to $60,000. We came close to raising it to $90,000 when we saw an increase in income as a result of some fairly favourable grain prices about four or five years ago. So in one sense there is a cap and in another sense there is not a cap.
Members should also know that within that legislation it is possible to apply for multiples. If a farmer has more than one or two people in his permit book, he can apply for multiples of up to three of whatever the coverage is. Currently, someone operating as a family farmer or as a limited corporation with more than one shareholder could be eligible for multiples of up to three. There is a case where in fact the cap, if you want to call it that, is certainly higher than $100,000.
I would also suggest it is very difficult in this type of legislation to enforce anything like this. I think the hon. member for Algoma made a very good point when he talked about some of the high value crops in the
Government Orders
horticultural industry for instance, where literally with four or five acres of crop, one could be very close to the $100,000 cap because of the value of the crops on that acre. Some horticultural crops not only have veiy high input costs but returns per acre. It is very difficult when we get into some of these things just to pick a number and say we want to stay with this.
I have one last point I want to make. A pretty strong argument against the cap is that we would find very quickly that producers-to the extent that they would want to participate in this program, and we think the interest is quite high-would very easily find ways of getting around this by simply organizing their affairs in such a way they had operating units that could each qualify for $100,000. They would make those kind of arrangements so that they could very quickly have a cap that is higher.
On a procedural or on a performance basis, I do not think that this type of a cap in legislation works very well. Whether we farm big or small in this country, we have freedom to own property. Whether the farm is 10 acres or 1,000 acres, the cost per acre is the same. I do not think we want to get into the business of telling people, either directly or indirectly, what size of farm they should have. It should be up to their own ability, their own management skills and their own ambition.
I think, for those reasons, that this type of motion is not the right regulation to have in this bill.

Mr. Speaker, there is considerable concern, not only in the agricultural committee but right across the country, relative to the actual responsibility of this legislation, because it is open legislation which does not, in any way, restrict the amount of money that can be spent or called on by the government after the agreements are signed.
I suppose these three motions are an attempt to put into the legislation some kind of responsibility to the taxpayers and recognize that certain farmers would benefit from the cap not being in place.
Let us take a look at the three motions. The argument concerning Motion No. 1 has been made often enough and long enough so there is no need to go further on it. Motion No. 3 deals with the ASA tripartite, hogs and cattle and so on. It would limit very large operators such as feedlots controlled by large multinationals from

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
receiving more than $100,000 per year of payments. If they received $100,000 per year, $67,333 of that would come out of the taxpayers' pockets. In other words, a $100,000 payment to a multinational which had afeedlot would get $67,333 from the taxpayers under the tripartite agreement. Is that what the taxpayers want?
Let us take a look at Motion No. 2. It deals with GRIP. This particular cap would have no effect on 95 per cent of the people who are likely to be in GRIP. I disagree with what the minister and the parliamentary secretary suggest. Large farms are not likely to divide in the short term. They might over a long period of time. To do so they would lower their coverage levels which they had accumulated over the last 10 years or so. That coverage comes from the good experience of crop insurance.
Only large farms operating below the production levels for their areas would divide their operations to take advantage of this sort of a situation. Other sections of the agreement are supposed to work against this kind of low productivity. It is not in the end a major effect even on that. It is unlikely that very many, if any, farms would divide to get more out of the program.
Many organizations which originally looked at this and suggested that there not be limits are now very concerned that there are not limits. They are concerned because they recognize that the danger to this program to a great extent is the fact it is uncapped. The danger to the stability of the program is the possibility that huge sums will be taken out.
We do not want to find ourselves in the situation in which the U.S. finds itself. In some of their programs 85 per cent of the payments go to less than 10 per cent of the farmers. That does not make farming a stable industry. This legislation is intended to bring stability to the farming community, to the industry. It should not have within it seeds for the actual instability which will eventually take place if there is a large extra payment for those of a particular size.
We are moving these motions for two reasons. First of all, the taxpayers deserve to have some responsibility in this legislation. I am sure the finance ministers would agree with that. Second, the seeds of its own instability should not be sown in the legislation so that eventually
the legislation will become less effective because of an action that we should have been able to change.

Mr. Speaker, my comments are directed to members of the NDP. Maybe they can through another member to respond to these points. The hon. member talked about multinational feed lots.
I am from the Lethbridge area and I am not aware of any multinational feed lots in southern Alberta. I am not aware of any in southern Saskatchewan. I wonder if the hon. member could tell us to whom he was referring. I did not think they were even covered by this statute because they have a tripartite program. We are debating the farm income protection act. How do his comments relate to this?
Second, the hon. member seemed to be saying with this cap that it would apply to a farm, but what about all of the communal farmers and people who operate in partnerships and so on, if we are going to have caps? If there are 20 families living on a communal farm or there is a partnership, would it not be limiting? Surely the hon. member does not intend that.

Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the House I will outline some of this for the member. First, this legislation does include ASA. It is rescinding the Agriculture Stabilization Act under which this tripartite agreement is written. It integrates it into this bill. Section 41(c), dealing with revenue insurance programs deals specifically with it. That is what Motion No. 3 is amending.
March 21, 1991

It is already in there. It is a tripartite thing, so that two-thirds of the pay-out comes from federal or provincial taxpayers. Bill C-98 rescinds the Agriculture Stabilization Act and integrates it into this bill.
The proposal of a multinational feedlot was simply a proposal. It was an example of what can happen and what has, indeed, happened in the United States.
The $100,000 cap does not apply other than to GRIP or tripartite pay-outs or to the NISA maximum account.
Crop insurance stays as it always has been, covered yield times market price, so that the example previous speakers from that side have horrified themselves with could not happen. The horticultural crops would be covered for most of the $1,000 an acre that was proposed. It would only be the price differential which is in GRIP that would be limited to payments of $100,000 maximum per year.
I think it is important to get that straight so that government members, at least, know what it is they are voting on. I regret that they were not able to follow it closely in committee. That is partly why we have report stage in the House, so that all members can get more acquainted with the bills.
These proposals do not apply to crop insurance coverage. They apply only on those programs that are on top of that which are effectively price insurance programs, such as GRIP, the tripartite programs and the income account under the proposed NISA. A 4,000 or 5,000 acre wheat farm that lost all of its crop would be largely covered by crop insurance. The GRIP portion for most
4,000	and 5,000 seeded acre farms would not be limited in the receipts by the $100,000 cap.
I have done the calculations for the coming year and there is virtually no wheat farm in western Canada that would have its payments reduced if they seeded 5,000 acres of wheat and had a 30 bushel coverage level.
The levels we are talking about reducing payments to are farms that are veiy large indeed. It is still possible, even if these amendments were put in, from my checking, for a integrated farm or a mixed farm that is in the feedlot business or hog business, as well as in crops, to receive maximum payments to $100,000 under the crop side and $100,000 under the tripartite side. In fact, the real limit is something more than $200,000, because that kind of an operation might be drawing out of its NISA
Government Orders
account that year as well. So these are veiy large sums of money coming from the public purse.
I think the government should reconsider whether to put some caps on this so that the tax paying public has some assurance that we have not all gone completely bonkers, even though it will not limit very many payments.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I do not want to set a precedent here.
We are into report stage. The parliamentary secretary started a question and comment period and the minister wants to reply. I would hope that maybe at the next motion, the hon. minister will have another opportunity. Otherwise, we will never get this done.

Mr. Speaker, I think the amendments proposed the hon. colleague for Mackenzie are very important, indeed. He has very eloquently outlined the reasons why.
There is a problem in the agricultural community these days with the future it is facing. Rural communities and family farms in this country are disappearing. They have been disappearing at an alarming rate for a long time.
The purpose of this amendment is to begin to change the attitude that this government and past Liberal governments have had to the future of family farms. If we are going to maintain a strong family farming structure, we need to keep that in mind when dealing with legislation.
The $100,000 cap is going to include most farmers who exist today in this country. The concern is that as agriculture becomes bigger and bigger business and corporate enterprises become more and more involved, there is increased vertical integration in the agricultural industry.
Cargill, for example, is a tremendous interest in the U.S. It is expanding every day in Canada. It is important that we place some limits. A $100,000 cap is, for most people, not a limit.
As the hon. member for Mackenzie pointed out, very few farms would be affected. Those would be only the very large farms.

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
The point that the hon. minister and other members have made in the past is that people will abuse the system, that they will be dividing their farms and so on. There is no program that is perfect. That is for sure. Certainly, this will not be either, but there are ways and means of putting in safeguards to keep that to an absolute minimum.
With respect to the program that is before us, many of the witnesses who appeared before us in committee agreed that there were ways to work the program. That is possible regardless of what type of program we have.
We have an unemployment insurance program and there are certain people who try to take advantage of it. We have a whole list of programs in this country that people attempt to take advantage of, but by and large most Canadians are honest and try and do comply with the rules.
The argument of not being able to put a cap in place simply because people will take advantage of the program is not a valid one. It is one the government should quit throwing out.
The other aspect is that this program is not a cost of production program. The smaller family farm is not getting full advantage of a cost of production program. In fact, it is going to lose out in the end. This program will be a very rich program, but it has been predicted that GRIP will go tremendously in the hole in the next two or three years. We are going to have a program in which we may find ourselves with some very serious problems in a few years.
The difficulty is that as the 15-year average goes down, we are going to find that farmers are paying a higher percentage of their average crop production, of their average income, and receiving less and less for it. That certainly is a problem. One of the fundamental flaws with this program is that it does not recognize that fact.
If we had a cap on this program and geared the program to the family type farm, the more average size farms in this countiy, we would all be better off. Certainly those farmers would be better off because it would be possible down the road, as this program is reviewed and re-evaluated, and perhaps changed to reflect that, to bring in a true cost of production up to a set level.
That is why these amendments are important. They are important because they set a new direction. As New Democrats, we applaud that type of direction. We cannot understand why the government and the Liberal Party would not support such an amendment. To us, it is an important factor in maintaining viable farming families. I hope the government will reconsider and place that proposal before the House and be willing to support it.
The other point that has to be included in this amendment is to keep in mind that as this program goes into the hole, as it goes further into debt and is reviewed down the road, there may well be changes to it in five years. As the government has said, it is going to enter into a review process so that farmers who have a program for five years may find that, because of the richness of this program, because of the fact that a few very large producers have received the full advantage of this program, all producers will suffer. Surely that is not the objective of this program. Surely the goal of this program is not to reduce the number of farms. It certainly seems to be the effect.
The way this government has manoeuvred agriculture in this country over the last six or seven years bears that out. This government set up an environment which will hurt average farms and rural communities. With the changes to the Wheat Board Act, this government's attitude and actions do not bode well for the future of farming in this country as we know it today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rod Laporte (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-98 be amended in clause 4 by adding immediately after
line 21 at page 3 the following:
"(b.l) the program should encourage the long-term social and economic sustainability of farm families and communities;"
He said: Mr. Speaker, since I was elected in 1988, I have had the opportunity to travel across this country. One thing I have noticed is that geographically, Canada is really a rural nation. We have pockets of population in various parts of the country. We have this so-called golden triangle in the Toronto area. We have the lower mainland of British Columbia. We have, I suppose, a population base in the Ottawa area. Outside of that we have largely a rural nation.
Even areas that Statistics Canada would include as urban are in fact rural. In my riding, for example, the riding of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, half the population lives in the city of Moose Jaw, which is considered urban by Statistics Canada, but in fact, it is a rural city. It depends on the rural infrastructure that exists around it, the economic infrastructure, the farmers and others who do business in Moose Jaw. There is an area which the city of Moose Jaw services.
There are many urban communities in this country which depend on rural Canada. This country was developed on a regional policy. Western Canada was settled because the government of the day desired that people should move to the rural areas of this country. In fact, that is why the west was settled. That is why people moved there. It is important to keep in mind that this country has largely developed on policies of government focused on regional development.
As I mentioned earlier, the problem we have today in this country is that we have a government that seems to have lost sight of that objective; I suggest it has clearly lost sight of that objective and that goal. We have a government now that is considered a bottom-line government, an open-for-business government. Tending to move toward a so-called free enterprise government is
Government Orders
really putting us back into the 19th century. We have a situation where rural Canada has suffered.
As I said, I have had the opportunity to travel around this country. I can go out to rural Nova Scotia, a rural community there, sit in a cafe and have coffee with some of the local folks, and I can have virtually the same conversation there that I can have in my home riding in rural Saskatchewan. People talk about VIA Rail being lost; they talk about post office closures; services closing up; seniors who do not want to stay in those communities because they do not have the services; young people who do not want to move there because there are not the amenities or jobs. The only difference that I find between rural Nova Scotia and rural Saskatchewan in many ways is the economic base. In Nova Scotia it is fishing or it may be a different type of agriculture, fruit and so on. In Saskatchewan, in my area at least, it is largely grain farming. The economic base in all those areas is suffering.
We have a situation where the infrastructure of rural Canada is in a very bad state. Rural Canada has been shrinking since the end of World War II. Now it is starting to collapse.
Unless we have a commitment by Canada and by this government to work toward maintaining viable farming families, viable rural communities and a viable rural infrastructure, that trend is going to continue. It is continuing at a disastrous rate that is going to have a devastating impact on this country.
In the province of Saskatchewan we have lost over
60.000	people, a net loss in the last four or five years. People have been predicting that Saskatchewan in the next 15 years is going to lose somewhere between
150.000	and 200,000 people. If anything anywhere near that actually occurs, the province of Saskatchewan will be in real trouble.
What do we have? We have had deregulation in transportation that has affected transportation in Saskatchewan. We have had a loss of railways. We have had rail line abandonment. We now have UNITEL which wants to come forth and change the whole communications system, which is going to have effects on rural Canada.
This amendment that is being proposed here simply requires the government to keep in mind, to take into account the long-term social and economic sustainability of farm families and communities. That is a statement I

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
would defy anybody in this House to get up and say is not a valid principle. It is a valid principle. Any member who does not support that principle really cannot say that they have the interest of rural Canada at heart. It is a fundamental principle that should have been in the legislation from the very beginning. It is a principle that so far this government has rejected. I do not know why. I find it extraordinary that it has rejected that principle. It should be in the legislation and it should be supported.
If we are going to maintain rural communities, if we are going to maintain farm families, then we have to be taking some direction to allow that situation to exist. I am not saying, to use the Saskatchewan example, that we need towns every eight miles and everybody living on a half section; that is not what I am saying. What I am saying is that we should be able to provide an environment whereby a family which wants to either live in a rural community or on a farm simply has the opportunity to do so. It is becoming more and more difficult all the time.
This legislation is going to be reviewed. This legislation we all agree has many problems with it, and we are going to find many other problems as we begin to work with it. It is important that when this legislation is reviewed, and as we change the legislation over time, and I hope to make some changes here at the report stage, or even if we do not, that this principle is kept in mind. What this does is require the minister and reviewers of this legislation to keep that basic principle in mind.
I simply conclude by saying that I hope the government can find its way clear to vote on this basic, fundamental and, dare I say, motherhood issue that we all deem, I would suggest, important.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment before us, put by the hon. member who just spoke, talks about the long-term social and economic sustainability of farm families. Clearly, nobody has ever seen the kind of ravages that have taken place in western Canada since the present government came to power. I believe that this amendment would be useful because it might remind the government of what has happened to small towns.
Last spring I had the opportunity to go back to the community in which I practised as a veterinarian in the late 1950s for several years. I could not believe the kind of displacement which had occurred in that community, which I had not visited for about seven or eight years.
During the last eight or ten years when the Prime Minister talked about being open for business, it certainly has not been open for business to assist those small prairie communities which have been ravaged so drastically in the last four or five years.
Even though this legislation does give some long-term hope to those prairie communities, initially it is not great, because we put down the motion on Monday calling on the government to immediately implement a third line of defence, a deficiency payment, cash to producers this spring for the current crop year 1990-91. The government has given no commitment. All it has talked about is how much deficit there is in each of the three major accounts: the Western Grain Stabilization Program, the Canadian Wheat Board account and the demand for a premium.
To that extent, the provisions in this bill for special circumstances, Committees Special Assistance, at this time, are a failure.
I guess one could say that the NISA program is a failure also, because none of the provinces, with the exception of Saskatchewan, are able to participate in it. The problem with NISA is that most farmers do not have the resources to put money into the account in order to qualify for assistance this year. Clearly the GRIP program does not really provide much benefit this year. There may be an initial payment this fall, but there may not be. It is totally a decision of the Government of Canada and the signatory committees.
As the hon. member has said, to some extent this is a motherhood issue. We feel it would be useful to put it into the bill. We want to support it because perhaps it would make the government more conscious of the fact that we are not just talking about producers of wheat, canola, other grains and oilseeds, but we are talking about stabilizing the whole rural economy so that there are stores, businesses and other people existing in these communities.
March 21, 1991

We always felt that Canada had that special ability. That is why we have had programs like the western grain stabilization fund. That is why we have a Wheat Board, because we want to bring stability. That is why we have marketing boards.
This government is hell-bent on cloning the whole great American dream. That system has not been great for those states like North Dakota and Montana and the northern tier of the states. I do not think that cloning of the American system is going to be great for Canada and for our western prairie producers. We think this amendment would be useful, because it reminds the government of its responsibility not only to individual producers, but also to the over-all viability of the rural communities and the rural way of life.

Mr. Speaker, when Bill C-98 was presented, it made an unusual but maybe a very acceptable difference in its approach to the whole program of safety nets and a considerable amount of legislation in that the bill contained a definition of what the government thinks or what the legislature thinks should be the aims of the programs being discussed today.
In that series of principles which it has placed before the House through this bill, the government has indicated a certain structure at which it feels agriculture should be aimed. Basically we as legislators should be keeping that in mind when we deal with agricultural legislation and when we deal with safety nets.
As I said earlier, this particular legislation provides or allows agreements between the provinces and the federal government to keep the structure of safety nets in place for the foreseeable future. It is very important, under those circumstances, to make sure that in the processes of review and of making decisions relative to this bill and to the agricultural industry we keep in mind the most important people as far as this matter is concerned. Those are the farmers out there who have managed to survive the ravages of the past few years and are hoping to be farmers 10 years from now or 5 years from now when the initial review happens.
In making those kinds of review, it is important that we have in place principles which do exactly what this amendment does. The program should encourage the long-term social and economic sustainability of farm families and communities.
Government Orders
If we were allowed to go back to the previous three amendments, we would say that they in themselves also contribute to the sustainability of long-term and effective farm communities, because they suggest that the massive consolidation of farm production should not be allowed to end up in the hands of multinational corporations.
Anything that encourages larger and larger developments should not be paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. If we allow the taxpayers of Canada to subsidize the large operations, we indirectly empty the rural areas of population. If the population is not there, the services disappear and eventually the communities themselves disappear.
That is why we think we should make sure by this legislation and subsequent legislation and by the agreements that are to be signed between the federal and provincial governments that farm communities and farmers themselves are the central figures in the thinking; not the production, not the export sales, but the life and survival of the farm family and the farm community.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):

speechtext:

That has been lacking for years, but we are addressing it. I believe that the farmers and producers of this country are very satisfied and that we will all benefit from this legislation.

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
Most of our farm enterprises are family owned farms. It is a given that a family farm is a very important part of the whole agricultural industry in this country. This bill provides for programs that will ensure economic and environmental sustainability of our agricultural sector. If we do not implement these initiatives, we will be threatening the very fabric of our farming industry.
I would like to quote Mr. Geddes of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture who was a witness at the Standing Committee on Agriculture on March 13: He stated: "The safety net program was designed to solve one of the situations in the rural economy for grains and oilseeds at this time, and that is income stability".

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will just speak very briefly to this very interesting motion.
Most of us who are connected intimately with agriculture would agree that the family farm is one of the
reasons we in this country and in other parts of the world have been as successful as we have in agriculture.
There are three brief reasons why I think this motion has some merit. First, any time somebody else pays 60 per cent of a premium and the farmer pays 40 per cent indicates support for farmers and for family farms. That is the situation here: the farmer himself will pay on average 40 per cent of the premium, the provincial governments will pay 25 per cent, and the federal government will pay 35 per cent. That in itself is support for the motion.
Second, the safety net programs are designed to make the assistance that is available more predictable. We have heard many times in the past that if farmers knew ahead of time how much money they were to receive from various programs, even though they received the same amount of money later on, that knowledge of the exact amount of money they were eligible for would have been of more use to them ahead of time for planning what types of crops to seed and the type of financial arrangements they make with their financial institutions. That provides some support and stability for farmers and for family farms.
The third point I would make very briefly is simply that once this bill is up and running, once the subsequent agreements are signed with the provinces, and farmers begin making use of these programs available under this legislation, the type of coverage and support an individual farmer will receive is going to be very much tailored to his own capacity to produce on that piece of land. If he wants to work harder, use more chemicals or use better weed control, put in some irrigation, intensify his cropping practices so that he can earn more off that piece of land, he will then have that extra income and capacity to produce reflected in the way the program operates.
To summarize very briefly, the very fact that the producer will be paying 40 per cent of the premiums and governments will be looking after 60 per cent, the fact that the program is predictable, more so than anything we have had to date, and the fact that it will be tailored to an individual farmer's capacity to produce on that piece of land indicate some pretty strong support for the individual farmer and for the way family farms operate in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on Motion No. 4, coming as it does in the section which sets out the principles the minister shall take into consideration in respect to any program he is
March 21, 1991

establishing in conjunction with the provinces. We had four principles outlined in the original bill and none of them mentioned anything about farmers. It talked about levels of protection and it talked about being compatible with Canada's international obligations. It talked about not unduly influencing the decisions of producers of agricultural products with respect to production or marketing, and it talked about encouraging long-term environmental and economic sustainability.
However, it did not mention farmers and it did not mention communities. It was a little uncertain as to whether government members when drafting this bill really considered farmers and small communities to be a natural part of the economic environment in the countryside at the moment.
This will help to clarify that. It may not change the kinds of agreements arrived at, we realize that. This bill will simply require that the minister take these principles into consideration. It does not say he has to follow them.
For that reason, I choose to spend a couple of minutes urging the minister to give fairly high priority to this business of making agreements that will be cognizant of the needs of both farmers and the people who live in villages and towns in rural Canada.
I am from Saskatchewan, the more settled part of the prairies which was part of the forest belt at one time. It is more heavily settled than the wide open plains, but we are still fighting the same enemies as rural people elsewhere on the prairies. Our enemy is distance. Distance creates problems for people whether they are living in a small village, in a town or in the countryside on a farm. It creates problems as to our ability to sustain basic services that we all need, whether we live in the countryside or whether we live in metropolitan Toronto.
Turning to health and medical care, when we have to go more than 30 or 40 miles to find a doctor, a nurse or even a drugstore, it creates some problems for raising families. It creates problems when we are old. It is not a situation that leads to people staying where they are. They tend to shift away from that area to where those services are more readily available.
Government Orders
There is the question of educational services. It is the same thing. Younger families look at how long their kids will have to be on the school bus. They have to consider whether the roads the school bus travels over are going to be open year round and make the decision whether to stay in the countryside, in the small village or to move to a larger centre.
For people who are operating farms, distance is our enemy when we seek repairs or marketing services. The last decade has virtually decimated farm equipment suppliers. In order to get parts for our ever aging machines, we have to go farther and farther afield. The suppliers have kept up to date as much as economic conditions will permit. They are hooked into computerized networks and can tell us on the phone whether they have the part, whether it is in Flint, Michigan or wherever it might be in North America or even in Europe, and how long it will take to arrive. When it comes we will probably have to drive 50 or 80 miles to pick up a needed part, taking two and a half or three hours not counting the delay for shipping. Given the current financial situation, most dealers cannot keep in stock every part we might want. It has to be brought in from a central depot or from the factory.
These tough economic times and to some extent policies which are encouraging consolidation of towns and villages are creating double costs for people who live in rural Canada.
We have to pay for the services that we built in the recent past. Most of those hospitals, schools and roads are still in the process of being paid for. Most of the roads are built on a pay as you go basis, but the water and sewer systems are not. As people leave for other provinces or to big cities in search of jobs or better service for their aged parents, or their young children, they abandon those capital investments and force the new communities to invest in new schools, new hospitals, new homes, more water and sewage systems, to accommodate the new populations while the already produced accommodations out in the towns and villages go under-utilized. It is not good economics. It makes for very poor social conditions now and in the future.
We think that the provinces and the federal government should be much more cognizant of these very real issues which are occurring in rural Canada, whether it is in Newfoundland, Vancouver Island, the prairies, rural

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
Ontario, Quebec, or the maritimes. This has to be part of the consideration in any of these agreements. We are therefore pleased to see that the government members and all parties seem to be willing to include this forgotten element in the final form of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in regard to Motion No. 4 and the theme that has been put forward.
It is important that we on this side respond and indicate that, contrary to the implication from the other side, this government does care about rural Canada and does care about the farm community. I think most people in the farm community are well aware of that, given the long string of initiatives which this government has put forward over the past six years.
Frankly, I find some of the rhetoric I have heard this morning a little bit disconcerting because there is a suggestion that somehow we can wish away reality. We have very difficult international circumstances. Over 80 per cent of the wheat grown on the prairies is destined for export. The world price has been decimated owing to the grain subsidy wars that have been going on between the United States and Europe. They have been mentioned before in this House many times and I am not going to go into the detail again. Suffice it to say that the world price is at a point where there simply is no return. That is why we have this enabling legislation to bring forward a new generation of safety nets which have been largely developed by producers themselves.
I do not think it is good enough to have a long litany of what is wrong from opposition members. What we would like to have is a little bit of co-operation from them in terms of saying what can be done. So far all I have heard is the suggestion of capping potential pay-out under these programs at $100,000 which the opposition already admits is meaningless.
What we need is something concrete. When the Liberal Party was in power in this country between 1968 and 1984, it did not do a whole lot for western agriculture. All I remember was the imposition of the capital gains tax which hung like a cloud over the farm community all through the 1970s and the early part of the 1980s.
This government, in living up to its election promise, got rid of that capital gains tax.
I remember the LIFT program that the former government brought forward. Perhaps the greatest legacy of all was a national debt in excess of $200 billion in March 1985. The requirement to pay interest on that debt at the present time would constrain any government in trying to bring forward the necessary programs and to sustain the kind of support that Canadians would want and, indeed, became very much accustomed to under previous administrations.
There is no magic in the movement of people from rural areas toward the urban areas. This is going on in every country in the world. It has gone on in this country since the rural population peaked back in the 1920s.
We are largely talking about the prairies this morning because that is where the dire consequences of this international grain subsidy war are being felt. The prairies were laid out under the Torrens land title system before many people moved west. The land title system was laid out in square miles before people came. It was laid out on the basis of the steam engine and the horse and wagon. Every five or six miles there was a stop for the trains to take on water. It was based on hauling 15 or 20 bushels of wheat a few miles from the farm to the elevator by horse and wagon. We have progressed a long way over the last 60 or 70 years.
As the member for Mackenzie rightly pointed out, we are gravitating towards a system where there are service centres every 30 or 40 miles that have the amenities that people want. That is because the people are already doing that. They are driving past the small towns, the villages-some of which never did amount to much; others which have declined over the years-in large trucks and semi-trailers. They are going to the larger places. The end result is that in a sense they are voting with their feet. They are causing a reality out there.
As the member for Mackenzie indicates, there has been a gravitation from having these communities every five or six miles, based on the horse and wagon, and based on the steam engine to the kind of system that we see evolving today. Indeed, if there were no people on the prairies right now, and we were laying out a grid system with towns and communities based on the technology, the communications, the road systems and all of the things that we know are possible today, these centres
March 21, 1991

would be laid out every 30 or 40 miles. It is exactly in accordance with the technology and with the wishes and decisions of people.
Having said that, yes, there is a need out there. The best thing that this government, or any government can do in terms of encouraging economic sustainability in rural areas and rural communities, is diversification. When I use that term diversification, it is not just in the sense of agricultural diversification. I am speaking about it in terms of things that are unrelated to agriculture, preferably completely unrelated.
That is where I would like to briefly touch on western economic diversification, because that is a $1.2 billion fund which was established by this government to encourage diversification in western Canada and on the prairies.
It makes loans, repayable loans to enterprises which have ideas, some technology, some innovation, some new products, some new markets which can replace imports. What it does is provide some much needed payroll jobs out there. Many of them are related to agriculture, it is true, but there are plenty of others that are not.
What that does is provide opportunity for people. It provides payroll. It enables them to stay in the smaller towns and in the prairie cities which have been so dependent upon agriculture.
It is important to recognize that significant contribution by this government through western economic diversification. It lends itself very well to the sentiment that has been expressed here and which we are all talking about and supporting. More important, it is not a matter of complaining, not a matter of a long list of problems.
We cannot do much about the world situation. We are at GATT. We are talking with the Cairns Group. I believe our people are doing all they can, but they are up against a couple of superpowers in the United States and the European Economic Community. We cannot wish that away.
What we can do, instead of whining and complaining, is come forward with initiatives like western economic diversification, which provides some much-needed variety in those areas. We can come forward with this enabling legislation, which is the subject of the debate
Government Orders
today. The farm income protection act legislation will enable the entering into of agreements for GRIP and NISA for the participating provinces and will provide the kind of long-term permanent safety net which is required out there. This will provide some much needed certainty and predictability for Canadians producers. That is something that is real and concrete. It is not a matter of wishes, it responds to a need and I encourage all members to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak for a few minutes on Bill C-98, and particularly to Motion No. 4 which stands in the name of my colleague from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.
I understand the minister and the government side are encouraged enough by the committee hearings and by the debate to accept my colleague's amendment which will at line 23 on page 3 of C-98, the words: "the program should encourage the long-term social and economic sustainability of farm families and communities."
It is obviously the kind of wording that is important in this kind of enabling legislation because enabling legislation is a process that allows for an agreement to be developed and to come afterwards. We do not really know what the final nature of the agreement will be that comes from Bill C-98, and that is one of the chronic problems with this kind of enabling legislation.
The government members keep saying that there is going to be certainty and predictability for those farmers and those farm families who make use of this legislation and these programs in the years to come. However, when one takes a close look at C-98 one does not find that kind of certainty and predictability and accuracy to which farmers are looking with increasing interest and need.
Other members have touched on the problems being faced in the grains and seeds sector particularly. We all recognize that the ongoing subsidy wars between Europe and the United States and others is making it very difficult for the sustainability of the Canadian farm as we know it. But there is another issue we have to address on the floor of the House today, that is adding the kind of wording suggested by my colleague from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. It gives some direction to this enabling legislation so that those ministers, bureaucrats and others who will be negotiating future instruments and

future amendments have some idea of what the intention of the House was.
As I understand it, members on both sides are going to be supporting this. It is important to have some idea of why this kind of wording is so important because we have seen in recent years, not only what my colleague touched on, but also the galloping nature of our national debt. It was less than $200 billion when the present Prime Minister came to office and, in June of this year it is going to exceed $400 billion. We see the time clock ticking away. The growth rate of the debt is on television regularly.
There are very few farm families in this country who also do not know the nature of debt and what kinds of problems come with it. My colleagues from Saskatchewan have touched on a number of both young and old who are being forced to leave the farms, not just on the prairies but also in areas such as the constituency that I represent, which is about one-quarter of British Columbia. It does not have the huge grains and seed acreages that one finds in the Peace, or in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba or other areas of the country, but there are farms and there are significant cattle producers and others in the area.
Don Rnoerr, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has appeared many times before the committee studying this legislation. I think it it is fair to say that he, like I, is concerned about giving the government carte blanche to do what it likes without really knowing what the final plan is going to be like and whether or not it will provide, what all members of this House would like to see, legislation and farm programs with long-term social and economic sustainability.
We have seen in recent years the closing down and the loss of a lot of federal institutions that have long been an important part of both rural and farm communities: the post office, train stations, branch lines and community grain elevators. We have seen a loss of much of the infrastructure which people who live in larger towns and cities take for granted, the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker disappear. All the different shops that were traditionally part of all of those small, rural communities have disappeared.
To an enormous extent, it has been as a result of uninterest and inactivity by federal governments year after year, government after government. They have not provided that little bit of additional financial and economic input that is required in a rural farm community to keep all those things going.
Once we lose a certain number of local enterprises, whether it is the person who provides seed or farm machinery or who fixes equipment or maybe does all those various things, we lose the critical mass.
Increasingly, on the prairies and in farm communities we are seeing a ghostly veil as more businesses close and more of these small communities wither on the vine.
As we see the problems on the international scale with the value that we are getting for our international commodity sales, we recognize as previous speakers have said that about 80 per cent of our grain sales are to offshore markets.
If we are not getting enough in terms of the costs of production, it means that those farms become less and less competitive and viable. The debt grows. More and more local businesses do not get paid, and it becomes a bit of a self-fulfilling prophesy.
That is why wording such as (b.l) proposed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre is so important as a guiding principle. If there are going to be certain things built into the agreements and amendments made in this five-year period before the Minister of Agriculture has promised that there would be another review, here is a guiding principle.
The bureaucrats, in particular, will be asking: What if we change this for this part of Saskatchewan? What if we changed it for this particular aspect? What would it mean in terms of the long-term social and economic sustainability? It is a very important principle to have in there.
As I said earlier, I am very pleased that it is going to be in the bill because there are many other problems which are threatening the long-term sustainability of the family farm in this country. Even the recent problems emanating from game farming, as you would know, Mr. Speaker, are a very serious threat not only to our existing cattle
March 21, 1991

Government Orders
operations but also to our wildlife populations in our national parks.
I have seen in recent days, for example, that a bred cow elk which had to be slaughtered because of a positive test for TB can bring a game farmer $7,000 under the federal pay-out scheme. The most one can get in this whole country for a cow, regardless of whether it is a Sementhal, a pure bred Angus or whatever breed that has to be slaughtered because of a positive test, is $1,500.
It does not matter whether the cow is worth $10,000 or $20,000. That is all you can get for a cow. There are special arrangements and agreements being made in relation to the game farming industry that also need to be looked at. They have not been looked at very carefully by this government.
All over the country, there are issues such as this cropping up for either the federal Crown or the provincial Crown. They have not been doing an adequate job of evaluating the impact and the problems of imports.
The hon. member for Mackenzie very recently raised the possible problems that could come from bringing in honey queens from Hawaii. We heard from the Minister of Agriculture that a group of investigators went to Hawaii to check and make sure that there were not mites and other problems with the honey queens coming.
How come you are wiggling your finger like that, Mr. Speaker? You are interested in knowing about Hawaiian honey queens. I recognize in the Peace district near where you live in Edmonton there is a need for additional bees. Many of them come from New Zealand and other areas. We are facing a shortage of bee queens.
As the hon. member for Mackenzie pointed out, the government seems very quick in wanting to bring in bees from Hawaii. We are facing chronic problems with infections in buffalo and elk. All of these things are threatening the traditional and important livelihood of our the farm economies, whether it is beef, grain, seed or dairy.
These are important things that the federal government should be doing to both monitor and evaluate before the problems become too severe.

Mr. Speaker, this proposed amendment requires the minister to place the federal-provincial agreements that are signed before the House within 30 days of being signed so that Parliament will have a chance to oversee what those agreements contain.

This is a second-best choice in terms of parliamentary overview of what is going on in the country. This body has the responsibility by tradition and by law to be responsible for the expenditures and the final decisions on how we tax ourselves.
Those decisions have gradually been eroded by practice over the last decade or so. Sometimes I fear we are getting almost to the point where responsible parliamentary government started, when parliament in the United Kingdom wrested power from the absolute monarch and began to take power unto itself so the people could decide where their tax dollars were coming from and where the money was to be spent.
We are coming perilously close to going back to those days with the very strong prime minister's offices that have developed over the past two or three administrations. This is definitely a second or third best option. It is only a requirement to have the government of the day report the agreements it has made beyond this Chamber back to the House. It would be much better if Parliament could pass legislation that would provide much clearer guidelines as to how those agreements should be made and what would be required, but that is not the choice of action in this particular era.
I would like to put on the record that I still find this reprehensible in terms of responsible government. It makes the job of all backbenchers and parliamentarians extremely difficult and frustrates the role they have traditionally had to play by having such open-ended kinds of legislation to deal with where, in effect, Parliament says to the executive branch of government: "Here, do whatever you like. Come back and report to us 30 days after you have done it".
I do not like that particular principle, but having the government report is better than not having it report, and that is basically what we are down to with this particular amendment. This motion suggests that members of Parliament, at least after the fact, bring in these agreements when they are in fact signed and lay them before the House. Ideally I suppose we would like it to be before the fact, but it sort of makes a small gain in terms of requiring the minister and the government to be accountable to the people of Canada for their actions. That automatically enables all members of Parliament representing all people of Canada to have access to the details of the agreement.
Not only does it do that, but in a sense it provides an element of accountability. The government is saying that it is quite prepared to recognize that these agreements

Government Orders

He said: Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 7 makes a provision in the NISA agreements that require that the producer participating in a Net Income Stabilization Account program must be a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident of Canada.
This is a program that would be judged by some people outside agriculture to be a very generous program. It is designed, I believe, to be a rainy day fund for producers who have a reasonable level of income, are able to put money into the Net Income Stabilization Account, and to receive support from the government not only in matching that contribution but in allowing them to put in a certain amount of funds over and above it to the extent of 20 per cent.
If we take the example of a farmer who has $500,000 worth of eligible production and there were two parties to that production, a husband and wife, then they would be eligible under the NISA program as I understand it. We do not actually have the agreements in front of us, but we have seen some of the publicity and the planning for it. Each one of those would be able to put into that account some $5,000, which would be matched by the government. Then the government would pay prime of
March 21, 1991

commercial rates on the portion that the government puts in and would provide prime or a commercial rate of interest plus 3 per cent on the $5,000 that each spouse put into NISA. This is assuming that they have eligible production costs of $500,000.
On top of that, producers can put in an additional 20 per cent. That means if they had the money-and not many farmers today would have it-they would be eligible. As the hon. member from south western Ontario said, they could borrow the money. They could put in an additional $100,000 and invest it in NISA at prime.
Let us assume that prime right now is 12 per cent. They would be paid 15 per cent by the government. On a $100,000 NISA, over and above the regular 2 per cent that they can contribute, they would be able to contribute another 20 per cent. If commercial or prime rates were 12 per cent or 15 per cent, they would be earning $15,000.
This is designed to provide stability over the long haul combined with the Gross Revenue Insurance Program. For many of the horticultural crops it will probably be extremely difficult or perhaps impossible to develop a plan that will qualify for GRIP. NISA has that advantage.
The other advantage is that even though the government says in its preamble to the objectives of the legislation that it is going to be acceptable in international fora, I do not know of anybody who really believes that the revenue guarantee part of GRIP will not be subject to attack by the Americans.
We have already seen this morning a report from one group, Wharton Economics Forecasting Associates. It is projecting a 10 per cent increase in cropping. Of course it is always a sore point with the Americans that we have support programs but we do not reduce our acreage.
The revenue guarantee side of GRIP, I believe in the long haul, will be subject to attack by the Americans. They attack everything that we do, whether countervail or some other activity, especially if it threatens their producers. That is one of the advantages of NISA. It probably would not be subject to that because it is neutral with regard to production and so on.

It seems to me that many Canadians would say this is a program that is very beneficial, it provides prime plus 3 per cent, it provides a fund where a farmer can put 20 per cent, plus 5 per cent if the funds are available, that this kind of program should not be extended beyond permanent residents or citizens of Canada.
