I rise to support the motion proposed by the member for Algoma. It applies to the NISA or Net Income Stabilization Account, and it would add a new subclause to clause 7. With the new numbering system that would become 7.(2).
This particular proposal would require that a producer participating in the Net Income Stabilization Account program must be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident.
It seems to me that this makes eminent sense, not only for the reasons spelled out by my hon. friend who just completed speaking, but it would reduce the liability of the taxpayers of Canada for making viable the incomes of farmers who may not even live in Canada but in fact operate south of the border, or perhaps other combinations. The other thing it does is assure Canadian taxpayers, who are going to be financing this particular program quite substantially, that their dollars are being recycled to Canadian citizens or permanent residents of this country.

The program at issue here sets up two accounts, an A account and a B account. At the end of each tax year a producer has the option of contributing up to 2 per cent of his net revenue for that year into an A account. The government will match those funds in the B account. The producer has an additional option, if he so chooses, to put an additional 20 per cent of his net revenue for that year into his A account; however, the Government of Canada will not match that contribution in the B account.
For purposes of administration, these two accounts are then effectively combined and any interest accruing to that account becomes the property of the participating farmer. That interest is guaranteed by the agreements to be prime plus 3 per cent. So it is a fairly enticing rate of interest that this combined account will bear, and that interest will be paid by the Government of Canada out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
In this program, from what we understand of the agreements that are being reached, it would be possible, according to the witnesses we had from the department, for a married couple to set up two NISA accounts for their farm-one for each, husband and wife.

As I recall, this applied as well to the NISA account. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to speak to

this motion. This is a good motion put forward by my colleague from Algoma, which calls upon this House to place some limitations on the possible spending that may occur under this bill.
A number of motions have been put forward dealing with that very issue. It is an issue which is of concern to Canadians, the idea of taxation, the idea of a deficit and the idea of the national debt. We must remind Canadians and we must remind our colleagues on the other side of the House that we are dealing with a very large program which deals with hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars.
The very last thing we would want to do, I would suggest, is to allow a non-Canadian citizen or someone who is not a resident of Canada to somehow take advantage of this program. That would not be useful or serve the purpose of any Canadian anywhere in this country. This motion is an attempt to limit this.
The motion is particularly concerned with the NISA account. As we know, the NISA account is designed as an individual account for the individual producer, so that in years when his or her income drops below a given level, the producer will be able to access the account.
The idea behind this account is that the government will provide matching grants up to a given level. That is encouraging for a producer in itself, but an even more encouraging factor is that producers will receive interest 3 per cent above the going rate. It will give the producer an extra incentive to put money into this account. It will end up being a savings account for the producer and an account that the producer can access at any time.
As the government puts money into the individual producer's account, that is the producer's own money, in essence. He or she is restricted in their access to that fund by a number of factors. As I said, the annual income of the farmer must be below a given level before they can access the account. They also have access if they quit farming or if they retire. They have access to that account which can help with respect to retirement.
It would be most unfortunate if non-residents or non-Canadian citizens were able to acquire that type of fund for their own purposes. In fact, there are ways potentially that this could be taken advantage of in a unfortunate fashion. Under this account, if a farm is incorporated, for example, and the company has shares
Government Orders
owned by various individuals, that company will have a NISA account. It is veiy easy for a company to simply dissolve itself. Of course, if the company dissolved itself, the money in that NISA account would then be divided among the shareholders of the particular company.
If that should happen, then that account is dispersed among the shareholders. Certainly if there are shareholders who are non-Canadians, they will be able to take advantage of that program.
There is also another possibility. Most people are honest people, but there are those who are not.
There are ways to take advantage of it. If there is a way for non-Canadians to take advantage of it that would be especially tragic. An individual producer cannot access that fund unless their income drops below a certain level or, they simply get out of farming. That is the only way they can access that account.
A corporation has a much bigger advantage, which is, as I said, that it can dissolve itself. Therefore, a farming corporation can acquire money into the NISA account, simply dissolve, take the money out, pay it to the shareholders and then turn around and form another company. There is a potential for some unfortunate advantages to take place in this. It is something that the government, I hope, is going to do something about. Certainly if there are non-residents who are involved in that company, this motion would certainly address that concern.
I think this is part of the larger concern of the need to have reasonable taxation and reasonable spending by the government. What we want is a government that is going to deal with the people's money with some care. Certainly the government is always making much of the fact that it is very fiscally responsible and a good financial manager. Well, this is a motion that the government would want to accept and adopt because it formally puts in place legislation that is going to block that particular loophole.
In various provinces throughout this country there have been concerns with foreign residents and non-Canadians involved in agriculture. It is a good motion and I would certainly urge the government to support it because if we are going to maintain some credibility in this country it is motions like this that must be passed. Mr. Speaker, I am not going to deny that the monetary policy of the country has an effect on the Canadian dollar, the level of the Canadian dollar.
However, I would point out to the member that in the last eight months there have been a number of changes in monetary policy which have resulted in a 4 per cent drop in interest rates, as well as a narrowing in the interest rate spread between the United States and Canada from a peak of 5.5 per cent to the current level of about 3.75 per cent on the 90-day commercial paper rate.
There have been significant changes in monetary conditions. These have been translated by the market into a drop in interest rates.
My hon. friend says that he would like to see a lower level of the Canadian dollar, but the market is operating in a way that is contrary to his wishes. Unfortunately his wishes cannot always be reflected in what the market does.

I have to assume, Mr. Speaker, from the minister's answer that the market is not responding in the way that he would wish either.
It is really the government's high interest rate policy that has resulted in the situation Canada faces today. That is the real reason for the gap between U.S. and Canada interest rates which has led to the situation where a growing portion of our national debt is now held by foreigners. Canada, as a result, loses a degree of freedom in its interest rate policy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take issue with the conclusion that my hon. friend just drew about what I said in my first response.
The point I was making is that there are many other factors affecting the level of the Canadian dollar than simply the interest rate spread between the United States and Canada or a certain level of in-flow of capital. Many other factors are taken into account here, and that is what sets the level of the Canadian dollar.
My hon. friend says that we have an increasing amount of foreign debt or debt to foreigners. The level of the federal government debt to foreigners is in around the 17 per cent to 18 per cent level. I ask for the indulgence of the House as I outline some important historical points which I believe, and hopefully you too, Sir, are vital to the question I raise today.
On September 25, 1989, the then Leader of the Opposition, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, rose on a point of privilege to protest the use of objectionable ads placed in newspapers across this country in late August 1989. In his able presentation, the then Leader of the Opposition made two substantive points. The first was that the ad prejudiced the proceedings of this House because the issue of the GST was still under debate in committee and the ad presumed the outcome of all parliamentary deliberations.
Privilege
The second important issue raised was that of contempt of Parliament based on the point that these ads diminished the authority and yes, Sir, the dignity of Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, you ruled that the arguments on prejudicing the proceedings of this House did not constitute a breach of privilege based on a thorough analysis and a definition of privilege found in Erskine May and other procedural authorities. However, Sir, on the question of contempt, the Chair stated on page 4460 that it was "in a quandary".
The claim that put the Chair in a quandary was, and I quote from Hansard again at page 4458:
-the advertisement is a contempt of Parliament because it infers that the House does not have any role to play in the passage of the tax and that it misrepresents to the Canadian public the procedures employed by Parliament in adopting legislation.
You, Sir, succinctly and precisely identified two items in the claim of contempt: namely, intent and content. As regards intent, your doubt was dispelled by the Minister of Justice at the time who at page 3821 of Hansard said that the ads were for informational purposes. This follows the tradition in this House that we accept the words of hon. members' explanations.
However, the Chair found that, with respect to content, and I quote from page 4461 of Hansard:
- the content was obviously drafted in a cavalier manner; there is an element of confidence, if not boldness-
The Chair concluded its remarks by sending a strong message to the Public Service and in particular, the Department of Finance. The message was that this country is a parliamentary democracy with the House of Commons at the centre of its deliberations. The ad was indeed ill-conceived and did a disservice to the "great traditions of this place".
With those five words "great traditions of this place", we on this side of the House certainly concur.
The responsibility of the Crown's ministers to inform the public, a long-standing convention of parliamentary democracy, ought to be practised on the floor of the House of Commons and not on the pages of national newspapers.
Today, I wish to raise several points as regards the latest ad campaign to sell the budget and, of course, to sell the Minister of Finance.

March 21, 1991
Privilege
I wish to present the arguments of the Minister of Justice in September 1989, which might be used today with the present application of contempt of the House. I do this because the situation is more serious procedurally today than it was in September 1989. The Minister of Justice argued in 1989:
The Finance Committee unanimously recommended to publicize details of the tax if the government were to proceed.
The budget had already been approved stating the government's intent to implement the GST by January 1, 1991.
That the Finance Committee was studying the issue and no case could be brought forward to show that it was being impeded.
That was in 1989. Those arguments cannot and ought not to be made in this particular case here today.
First, the finance committee has not unanimously agreed on the contents of the budget. Second, the budget has not been approved by the House and in point of fact, it is still under debate and we are not certain whether or not there will be a vote on the budget before we prorogue in May. Third, the finance committee is not dealing with any of the substance of the budget in this particular case.
The Department of Finance, in placing this advertisement in newspapers across the country, acted as if the House had already passed the budget. It is again a cavalier, deliberate approach contravening the proceedings of this House. Some would call it absolute arrogance in light of your ruling, Mr. Speaker. And not only did the ad presume that this House had passed the budget of February 26, it misrepresented the budget document tabled in the House of Commons by the Minister of Finance.
In September 1989, the then Leader of the Opposition, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra said, and I quote:
A government that wastes millions and millions of dollars on newspaper ads not even a canary would want to see on the floor of its cage, and keeps saying that it is trying to cut spending in order to reduce the deficit-that government is both hypocritical and utterly ridiculous.
Those words ring clearly today as we discuss this particular issue.
I refer the House to the 19th Edition of Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, page 145 under the section of
Constructive Contempts, subsection of the Publication of False or Perverted Reports of Debates, and I quote:
Analogous to the publication of libels under either House is the publication of false or perverted, or of partial and injurious reports of debates or proceedings of either House of committees of either House or misrepresentations of the speeches of particular members.
In the ad, under bullet point no. 2, the government states that it will, and I quote: "channel all GST and privatization revenues to a Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund". I wish to refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the budget document itself tabled by the Minister of Finance, page 78 in the English version, the last two paragraphs, to show this House and Canadians how the Department of Finance and the Minister of Finance have misrepresented his own words in this particular ad, and I quote for you, Mr. Speaker, from page 78 of the budget document, the English translation:
The Prime Minister has given a commitment that any above-projected revenues from the GST will make a contribution to deficit reduction rather than provide the leeway for an expansion in discretionary government spending. To implement this commitment, the government will introduce legislation to establish a specified purpose account, to which will be credited net GST revenues and from which will be debited public debt charges.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I table that for your subsequent reflection in making your adjudication.
In the minister's speech on page 13 he did suggest that all the revenues from the GST would go to the new debt servicing and reduction fund, but it is on page 78 in the details of the budget that the minister says what he really plans to do. That is where we learn that only above projected GST revenues would go to the proposed fund.
At page 78 the Minister of Finance even cites the Prime Minister of Canada, his own words on the subject matter. The ad's assertion that all GST revenues will be committed to the proposed debit servicing and reduction fund is completely inconsistent with the details of the budget document. Further, this assertion leaves the distinct impression with the reader that this fund, whatever its precise nature, already exists.
This is simply not true. In fact the legislation that the Minister of Finance proposes in his budget has not only not been adopted by this House, not only not been debated, but it has not even been introduced by the government. In addition, the advertisements claim that

direct program spending increases to the unemployed will result from the budget is also not supported by the document tabled before this House. Not only is there no new program for the unemployed, there is in fact a cut in the Canadian Jobs Strategy, a program which supposedly benefits the unemployed.
Any increase in the federal government's spending on the unemployed this year will not be a result of the 1991 budget, but rather a requirement on the part of the Government of Canada under the Unemployment Insurance Act passed by this House some decades ago.
It is obvious, sir, the intent and content of the framers of this ad. We know that budget documents are complex. They are lengthy and difficult to read. Canadians are not always going to take the time to read these documents. We felt that something that is condensed into eight pages of fairly direct language will help people gain that understanding. I might say that there is a very great demand for this information.
As an example, in the goods and services tax, the Consumer Information Office has sent out five million documents related to the goods and services tax. That gives us some sense as to the demand on the part of our voters for this type of information.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I must say I am grateful to my colleague, the House leader of the Official Opposition, for having brought to the attention of the House the contemptuous nature of the expensive and misleading advertising campaign which promotes the economic policy of the government, which misrepresents the budget that is before this House, which prejudices the decision of this House on the budget and which prejudices debate on this issue. Once again I compliment my hon. friend on his very thoughtful presentation to you, Mr. Speaker, on this very critical matter.
Before I begin, I want to say simply to my friend, the Minister of Finance, that I recall the GST mailings in terms of the evaluation that followed that, how effective that campaign was, and informing Canadians on the importance and the intricate nature of the GST. As to whether they understood it better as a result of receiving this documentation, I think the overwhelming evidence was that that was not the case. I suggest that the need to have sent out five million documents in response to inquiries simply points out the confusion that surrounds the implementation of this new form of taxation.
In light of the comments and arguments made by my hon. friend, the House leader of the Official Opposition, I have really only a few comments to make. With your
March 21, 1991

indulgence, I will focus on only two brief points: first, the wilful intent behind this advertising campaign and the fact that it exacerbates the contempt that we are presently discussing and, second, the attempt to deny this House its conventional and historic rights to pronounce itself on the budget.
I must say that this advertising campaign is not only part of a carefully designed media strategy but is part of a deliberate flaunting of the dignity of this House and its role and authority to permit the implementation of budgetary policy. I am afraid we have been reminded that this is not the first time members of this House have had to voice their concerns about zealous government administrations eager to put their spin on the matters before the House.
Fundamental to this whole issue is the question of why we are here. We are here because hundreds of years ago someone had the good sense to say no, to say that kings and other despots did not have the right to spend our money, to raise our taxes, unless and until we gave them that right. It does not matter whether it is a king or a prime minister or a deputy minister of finance who tries to usurp that right; this House and each of us in it must fight to defend that principle. You, Mr. Speaker, are of course the standard-bearer in that fight.
My colleagues have argued that the information distributed to every Canadian doorstep misrepresents the budget laid before this House. I support your arguments, Mr. Speaker, and the arguments we have heard earlier today. My concern is equally focused on the purpose behind this media campaign. Why did officials of the Department of Finance choose to give each Canadian household a copy of this flyer? Why did they choose to send it before the House had pronounced itself on the budget? Were they, as my hon. colleague has pointed out, not listening to you when you told them on October 10, 1989, and I quote:
I expect the Department of Finance and other departments to study this ruling carefully and remind everyone within the Public Service that we are a parliamentary democracy, not a so-called executive democracy, nor a so-called administrative democracy.
Privilege
Let us look at this recent history to which your comment refers. In the summer of 1989 the government launched an advertising campaign in support of the goods and services tax. When the House returned that fall, the former Leader of the Official Opposition raised with the Speaker the contemptuous nature of those advertisements. While you, Mr. Speaker, did not find that there was a prima facie case, you offered some very stern warning to those who implemented the campaign to which the opposition took offence. You said you had to ponder the intent of the offending advertisement as compared to its contents.
In light of the Minister of Finance's assurances that the intent was to inform Canadians and not to diminish the dignity of the House, you found that there was no contempt.
However, Mr. Speaker, you concluded with the comments:
I expect the Department of Finance and other departments to study this ruling carefully and remind everyone within the Public Service that we are a parliamentary democracy, not a so-called executive democracy, nor a so-called administrative democracy.
I emphasize that particular comment of yours, because it should be remembered that today's offensive advertisement was drafted by that same department that you had specifically warned in December 1989.
I submit that the publication of which we speak contains a number of errors. In terms of the goods and services tax it says:
All revenues from the goods and services tax will flow into a debt servicing and reduction fund.
I give creativity marks to my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, who has tried to explain that. While the budget proposes to channel only net revenues, this certainly implies something contrary to that notion.
Also, the statements in this document say that the budget will cut the cost of government including salaries, and yet the government's own estimates show that it will actually spend more money this year than last.
It says that the budget will direct program spending increases to the unemployed. We all know that the unemployed can rely on the self-financing employment

March 21, 1991
Privilege
plan. Of course we see no new programs and have actually had the announcement that the Canadian Jobs Strategy will see $100 million cut from it.
In closing, I want to say that the Minister of Finance and his officials knew the rules, and they understood your ruling. They could only have been deliberately disregarding this House and the role that I, members opposite, members beside me and you, Mr. Speaker, play.
I might add that the Minister of Finance and his officials also knew that there is no obligation to bring a budget before the House at this time but, having done so, the House has many rights over that budget. This is my final point. These include the right to debate the budget, to decide on the budget, to defeat governments on the basis of the budget, and to withhold passage of legislation based on the budget until a decision has been made.
Why, then, did the Department of Finance not wait until the budget debate had been concluded and the final budget voted upon?
Why did they not correctly reflect the material in the budget? I say that this is a wilful contempt of the House, a wilful contempt of your ruling of October 10, and deliberate disregard for the dignity and authority of this House.
On examination of this issue a number of questions are raised. I submit that the officials in finance did not wait for the budget debate to be concluded because they knew it would not be concluded. They knew that this House would never have the opportunity to vote on the budget. What greater prejudice to the proceedings of this House can there be than to do away with these proceedings?
It would appear, even by comments made earlier today, that the government does not plan further debate on the budget motion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising from the business of a committee. This occurred earlier this morning.
Of course, Mr. Speaker would be tempted perhaps to remind me that under our traditions committees are masters of their own business. While that is generally true I want to remind you of citation No. 569.(1) of Beauchesne's, fifth edition, which says:
Committees are regarded as creatures of the House and are governed for the most part in their proceedings by the same rules which prevail in the House with exception as to seconding of motions, limiting the number of times of speaking and the length of speeches.
It further says under 569.(2):
Committees receive their authority from the House itself and that authority of the House overrides that of any committee.
Mr. Speaker, I am bringing this issue to your attention for the following reason. The committee this morning was meeting under Standing Order 108(2). I bring to the attention of the House, and perhaps I could table the following, although it is available to officers of the House, the convocation asking members to attend the committee which states as follows: "Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations, pursuant to Standing Order 108(2) consideration of the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future." Very clearly, the committee was meeting under Standing Order 108(2) this morning to consider the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future as the notice published for us by the clerk indicated.
When the committee met this morning, it became aware of a certain report of the Citizen's Forum on Canada's Future. That report, which was made public last night, was later upon the motion of a member of the committee, duly moved and seconded. The report in question was tabled with the committee.
When hon. members immediately afterwards attempted to question the witness on the report itself, the chairman of the committee ruled that members could not ask a question about a public report, and at that a
Privilege
report which had already been tabled before the committee in question.
Mr. Speaker, the point I am making to you is that if that authority does not exist within the House itself, and I remind Mr. Speaker of what he has told us on several occasions in the past, that members in this House should be permitted to ask questions in a manner which is unhindered, providing of course that the Standing Orders and our rules and forms are adhered to. If that is the principle which guides us in this House, I fail to see how that principle can be overridden in one of our committees by a committee chairman.
Recognizing the authority the committee has to be master of its own business, nevertheless a committee or a member of a committee, in particular a chairman, cannot exceed an authority in the committee which Mr. Speaker cannot exercise in this House here, or does not exercise in this House here.
I am not expecting an immediate ruling on the issue. I conclude my remarks by asking Mr. Speaker to review the transcript of the committee in question and to rule on the issue in question.

Mr. Speaker, I think that after reviewing the information I just brought to your attention, you will agree that the customary procedure of this House, as indicated in Beauchesne's and in the Standing Orders of the House of Commons, was not followed this morning. I think parliamentarians have a right to ask questions about a public report, a report that was tabled before our committee and that was under consideration by the committee, pursuant to Standing Order 108(2).

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to seek a clarification from you of a matter which was raised in the House on Tuesday of this week and on which you ruled on March 19. At page 18684 of Hansard with respect to the point of order I brought up at that time having to do with the question of confidence as it pertained to opposition day motions, you said:
The question of confidence, of course, lies with the government. The hon. House leader has made the position of the government very clear.
The problem with the position of the government was that the matter of confidence did not lie with the government. The position of the government was that the matter of confidence resided in the Standing Orders. This was the argument made very clearly and repeatedly on that day by the government, not only by the Government House Leader in response to my point of order, but also by the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare in his own speech to the House that day, in questions he put to the member for Winnipeg North and again in Question Period.
What I want to do is take the House through the two Standing Orders, the relevant ones prior to the McGrath reforms and the ones after. Those reforms came about as a result of the government, the same government which exists today, endorsing the recommendations of the McGrath report with respect to changing the rules of confidence in the Standing Orders. The government said on October 19, 1985, with respect to the confidence convention:
The government endorses the recommendations in principle. The government will seek to have a definition of confidence written into the Standing Orders to make it clear which votes are critical tests of a government's ability to maintain the confidence of the House: e.g., Speech from the Throne and Budget. The government will determine what legislation it will consider a matter of confidence.
Privilege
The government will also seek to have confirmed in the Standing Orders, the practice of votes independent of party position.
The Standing Orders as they existed prior to the government accepting that recommendation and prior to the implementations of the reforms, read as follows, and I am referring here to Standing Order 58(9):
In each of the periods described in section (5) of this Standing Order, not more than two opposition motions shall be-
And here is the key wording, Mr. Speaker,
-no-confidence motions against the government.
There, Mr. Speaker, is clearly the language of confidence in the Standing Orders with respect to opposition day motions. That was a problem that was identified by the committee as creating the context in which both opposition and government could hide behind the substance of motions.
After the McGrath reform, the Standing Order then read, and I read from that same Standing Order, section 9:
In each of the periods described in section (8) of this Standing Order, not more than four opposition motions shall be motions that shall come to a vote, provided that not more than eight opposition motions in total shall be motions that shall come to a vote during the three supply periods-
The difference is that in the Standing Orders after the 1985 reform, there was no longer the language of confidence with respect to opposition day motions. They were simply referred to as matters which would come to a vote, a vote which would be freer than the votes which used to take place in the context of opposition day motions, because the language of confidence was deliberately and self-consciously removed from those Standing Orders as a result of the reforms advocated by the McGrath committee, accepted by the government and incorporated into the new Standing Orders.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I take you back to your own ruling in which you said: "The question of confidence, of course, lies with the government." Exactly, because the question of confidence no longer lies in the Standing Orders. It lies with the government. Yet the argument that was being made the other day was directly contrary to your ruling and an argument which I suspect will continue to be made. The argument is that somehow or other the government is not permitted to vote for opposition day motions with which it happens to agree, such as the one the other day in which the government said it agreed that this House ought to reaffirm medicare, but it could not vote for the motion.

Mr. Speaker, the motion that we are debating is again an indication that obviously, but maybe surprisingly, it is the opposition members who are taking a responsible approach to this particular piece of legislation. Maybe this extends to their responsible approach to what we, as legislators, should be taking toward all movements within the government.
That is, this particular motion is limiting to some extent the possibility of advantage being taken by people or organizations beyond what would ordinarily be the intent of the bill.
The motion states:
That Bill C-98 be amended in Clause 7 by adding immediately
after line 27 on page 7 the following:
"(1.1) A producer participating in a net income stabilization account program must be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident."
It seems that this is obviously reasonable and eminently logical because the intent of Bill C-98 is stabilization of the agricultural industry within Canada. It is not intended to be the stabilization of a particular farm by someone who owns that farm, but who lives outside the country.
We recognize that if he is a permanent resident, it is an acceptable part and recognition of the fact that he is contributing and paying in Canada. However, if he is not a citizen or a permanent resident, then he will not, in the event of taking advantage of these operations, be doing so to the advantage of Canada. We recognize and hope that this is not an extension. Most or all of the people who fall into this category are just south of the border and farm on the Canadian side.
Government Orders
NISA, the Net Income Stabilization Account, is a surprising bit of legislation under any circumstances in that it is a glorified RRSP in some ways as far as farmers are concerned. It is glorified in the sense that no other RRSP across Canada has the government matching the contributions that the farmer makes into it. No other RRSP guarantees a certain level of interest return.
That is a very specific bit of ability on the part of the government if it is acceptable to the taxpayers generally of assisting a farmer who is in a situation where some place down the line he can use money that was maybe a little in excess a few years before. The contributions by the government increase it enough to make it a worthwhile operation.
We have to recognize that it is using taxpayers' money to match funds put into the specific account and that we are also guaranteeing a specific return, which I understand is 3 per cent above the prime rate. You, Mr. Speaker, would be happy with such an RRSP.
Why are we giving this kind of specific help in extending it to people who do not live in Canada and who are not citizens of Canada? The particular fund account is divided into two specific accounts, one of which is after tax: The producer part is after tax. The second fund, which is a specific section or will be kept separately, will be kept for the contributions by the government or governments-because the provincial government may also make contributions to this fund- and to the interest that is raised. In other words, it is set up in such a way that the farmer portion of it, which is put in after tax, and the government portion are kept separately. But both portions are going to be available to the farmer if he decides he needs them or if he qualifies for them.
If you are my age, Mr. Speaker, that qualification might be within a couple of years. So it is a particular situation which I think needs to be looked at. I compliment the member for Algoma in making sure that we in this legislature have taken a good look at limiting wherever possible the waste, the misuse that can come out of this.
It also relates back to the original three motions which were before this House that suggested that the total amount returned from any of the accounts here-NISA,

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
GRIP or the income revenue account-all be limited so that there would not be the excesses that are possible under the present legislation.
There is no doubt that the legislation itself, the structure under which this legislation is developed, the direction that it goes in making sure there is some kind of a net for the farmer, is acceptable. But if you link these moves in such a way that specific people who do not qualify, do not need, then it quits being a safety net and it becomes a method of giving money to people who should not be getting it.
That is what this particular clause does and what the other clauses that we objected to earlier, or which we think should be put in, also do.

The
motion moved by my colleague from Algoma restricting the receipt of benefits from and participation in the NISA section of this Farm Income Stabilization bill I think is one worthy of serious consideration.
As has been pointed out by other members of the House, what we are doing is making this part of this program available to people who are not necessarily citizens of this country. This is a good part of the act, it is a very generous part of the act, and once in place will serve a very useful purpose, and hopefully will bring some more stability to the farm income situation that has gone on far too long in this country.
It is a part of the act that is going to require a considerable number of taxpayers' dollars to make it successful, with contributions from both the provincial and federal governments as well as from the participants themselves. I think we have to give some serious thought to this -not that we don't necessarily want foreign ownership of farms. If one wanted to be cynical, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if this is because of the benefit this would give to foreign owners as well as to Canadian ownership. I wonder if this is a message that the present government is sending to foreign owners, that if they get involved in the Canadian farming operations they can benefit from this type of program. I hope that is not the case, and I do not think that is the case, but it certainly would be looked upon and can be looked upon by potential or present foreign ownerships as a veiy beneficial way of bringing money, and it does allow them to bring money, from outside the country into the country to receive a basic interest plus a bit of a premium on that.
This could be very beneficial for them. This would be at the expense of Canadian taxpayers.
I do not think the Canadian taxpayer has any strong objection to this type of program being put in place to lend stability to Canadian producers. That, quite frankly, is the purpose of this bill. However, I do not think it should be available to those who are not Canadian citizens or are not permanent residents of Canada. I am not at all sure that we are doing ourselves or the industry justice if we leave this out. I feel this amendment is needed in the bill to make it proper and to make it fair for Canadian citizens and for Canadian taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, wish to speak in support of Motion No. 7 introduced by my friends from the Liberal Party.
As my colleague from Saskatoon-Humboldt pointed out, while we support the broad outlines of the legislation before us, the draftsmanship of it is so wanting that we are very much afraid that within the legislation carries the seeds of its own destruction. There are so many loopholes and so many opportunities for abuse in the legislation that we are dearly afraid that the cost of this program is going to accelerate way beyond what the estimates now are and because of that, the program will self-destruct.
We expected and we hoped for good legislation. It is something that this government has promised western Canadian farmers for many years now. I remember well the former Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Wise, in 1985 promising us a comprehensive farm assistance type program. It has taken the government, through many droughts, price wars and political campaigns, to finally come to Parliament with certain proposals with its legislation. It is amazing to us, given all this time, how faulty this legislation is.
Of course the problem that Motion No. 7 addresses is a serious one. It might not be significant in terms of total dollars and cents, but it will certainly drain money from the public purse to benefit individuals whom I am certain no member of this House on either side of this Chamber would want to see money going to, namely some of those folks who live and are citizens south of the border who farm in Canada and would benefit under this program. Surely no member of this House on either side believe that this program is intended to benefit those types of individuals. Surely one has to be a Canadian citizen or a
March 21, 1991

permanent resident of Canada to be able to seek the benefits of the legislation in front of us today.
It is this type of sloppiness that creates this type of government waste that the people back home are furious about. They expect something a little better from Parliament. They expect something a little better from our political system. They certainly expect something a little bit better from the Conservative government.
I think it astonish the farm folks back home, many of whom support the Conservative government, many of them who hoped that in 1984 with the defeat of the Liberal government that finally the concerns of western Canada would get a decent hearing in the Parliament of this nation. High on their priority list was some legislation that would introduce a permanent program to protect western agriculture from the ups and downs of the price wars that existed between the treasuries of Europe and the United States. As well, they would like some protection from the ups and downs of our weather and the uncertainty that this provides to western agriculture.
We know in the west that we can grow good products, products that the world needs. In the long term there will a market for those products. Those products can and should be sold at prices that would sustain an agricultural economy, that would sustain family farms back home.
What they were asking for generations from the national Parliament was some well thought out programs that would put into place some of the permanent guarantees, some of the permanent stability, to ensure that our farm families will be able to withstand the downturns and enjoy the upturns.
The legislation that we have in front of us today, Bill C-98, fails to do that. It is with deep and profound regret that the farmers in Saskatchewan-and dare I say farmers right across the country, many of whom were historic supporters of the Conservative Party-feel a tremendous sense of disappointment, disillusionment and betrayal by this party and this government.
When one gets back home, it is amazing to see the sense of hopelessness and the sense of cynicism that people have concerning our institutions, particularly our
Government Orders
federal Parliament and our federal government. When we look at Bill C-98, at the loopholes that are incorporated in that bill and at the shoddy draftsmanship of that bill-I understand even the bureaucrats shudder when they look at the bill-we can begin to understand why the folks at home are becoming so cynical of the whole political process. They feel that they are not being listened to, that they have become marginalized.
On several occasions I have talked with farmers back home who have told me that they have voted for that party all of their lives, that their kids and their wives have voted for them. "But this is the last time", they tell me. They feel betrayed. They feel that we did not get a government in Ottawa that understood their needs and that was able to act on their needs.
It has taken a long time, from 1984 with the election of this government to now, almost seven years, for the government finally to get around to introducing the legislation the west has been wanting for such a long time. However, when it introduces the legislation, it is a piece of legislation that is totally unacceptable. It has within it its own seeds of destruction through the loopholes, the wastefulness and the exploitation that it would encourage. One wonders whether this party and this government really understand the needs of western agriculture.
My party has also introduced motions in this House. Motion Nos. 1, 2, and 3 attempt to put a cap on the program, to make certain that a few people will not get a large amount of the benefits from the public purse. I understand that up to 90-some per cent of the farmers who would be eligible for this program would fall under the cap of $100,000.
It is a means of ensuring that public moneys are well spent, that there will be the maximum benefit to the maximum number of people, rather than have it so open ended that there will be a few individuals who will be able to farm the system rather than farm in a manner that makes environmental and economic sense.
It is a piece of legislation that is full of loopholes, that has been sloppily designed and that deserves some major modifications. Therefore I also wish to indicate my support of Motion No. 7.

Government Orders

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will keep ray remarks confined to Motion No. 7 wherein it indicates that it must be a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident.
It is very easy to diverge and respond to some of the comments that have been made. However I will not do that at this time.
Under the current legislation we have in place many programs in support of agriculture, such as the WGSA, the Crop Insurance Program, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and so on. They recognize those producers who have farmed in Canada, regardless of their citizenship and/or the country of their residence. That has always been the case.
We have to recognize that we have a border which we share with the United States. It is probably the longest free-standing border in the world. We have several producers who live near the Canadian and American border on both sides and farm in both countries. Canadians are not excluded from U.S. programs, and we do not intend to start a system of cross-border exclusion.
For NISA, a producer must file a Canadian income tax form to be eligible to participate. In this case, a non-resident must report income earned in Canada and conversely become eligible under support programs.
To do anything different from this would not be consistent with other legislation we have. For this reason the government cannot accept this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering if a member of the government was going to respond to this very favourable and positive amendment put forward by the member for Algoma.
I saw, as I rose in my place here, the member for Algoma rising as well. He probably had a few things to say to the hon. parliamentary secretary in response to his response. Therefore, I will try to keep my remarks brief as well, to allow the mover of this motion perhaps to respond briefly to the parliamentary secretary.
I want to say a couple of things. First of all, I find it quite astonishing that the government is quite prepared to put away funds through this legislation, through the
NISA account, for American citizens. As the parliamentary secretary indicated, this legislation is not any different from the Western Grain Stabilization Act or other acts. That does not necessarily mean that if they have made one mistake on one occasion they should compound it by continuing to make that mistake in other legislation.
As far as I am concerned, the NISA program has many faults and problems with it. I will deal with that in other circumstances. However, one of the faults with NISA is that it does not limit the matching accounts, government funding, taxpayers money, to Canadian citizens.
As I indicated earlier today in remarks in this House on the motions that have been put forward by a number of members, I feel very strongly that the NISA account is a reward for wealthy producers in this country and does not address the farm problems that are compounding the financial crisis at the farm gate.
I do not believe that the government has the intention of trying to solve the farm crisis in Canada, because the programs we see seem to continue to compound those problems. As I indicated earlier, the fact that there is a $22 billion debt in agriculture in this country is not being addressed by this legislation at all. In fact, no legislation since this government has come into power has addressed the growing farm debt problem.
There has been a number of attempts to address the income problems. Those obviously have been inadequate, just as the GRIP and NISA programs will prove to be inadequate because they are not addressing the long-term financial crisis that affects the individual farmers at the farm gate.
Certainly we have a world marketplace problem that must be addressed. The Americans are a big part of that. The fact that this legislation will allow Canadian taxpayers' money to go and sit in American accounts to exacerbate further our anger with the American farm bill is just atrocious.
The government opposite is refusing to accept what I think is a very simple, reasoned, and logical amendment. It simply restricts the payments on this account to Canadian citizens or permanent residents. It is perfectly logical. We in Saskatchewan have had a long history of
March 21, 1991

trying to protect Saskatchewan farm land from foreign ownership, particularly American ownership. Not only are we now prepared to accept Americans farming our land. We are also prepared to help them retire in California, New Mexico, or Arizona by matching funds that they are able to put away. It just astounds me.
We fought prior to the 1988 general election the issue of free trade. Agricultural producers in Saskatchewan, for the most part, voted against the free trade deal. We did not like what was being proposed to us in terms of agricultural matters.
We felt that the American agricultural industry was putting too much pressure on the Canadian system to allow for long-term development of the agricultural sector in Canada. We felt that if Canadian producers were going to continue to be successful in the world market and to maintain our markets world-wide we somehow had to prevent the Americans from doing what they are continuing to do, despite all efforts to the contrary: to take our markets and move their products and obviously their people into our areas.
The Farmland Security Act in Saskatchewan was designed to protect Saskatchewan farmers farming on their own land. This government and its Conservative buddies in the Government of Saskatchewan who will be there for a short period of time longer, I suppose, are doing everything they can to ensure that Saskatchewan farmers get the short end of the stick. This simple amendment corrects a major problem with a major flaw in this legislation. It would be very simple for the government to say: "Okay, we are only going to pay money to Canadian citizens". That makes a tremendous amount of sense to me.
I did not have the opportunity to sit in on a lot of the standing committee testimony that was provided when the Standing Committee on Agriculture met. Therefore I was quite surprised when I saw this amendment brought forward on the Order Paper. Like most people I had reasoned, without having to look for it, that the government simply would not be providing funds to non-Canadians either in the NISA or in pay-outs to GRIP. I am very grateful to the hon. member for Algoma for discovering this in the legislation, recognizing that something was not there which to my mind should be. It just had to be there.
Government Orders
For an act to allow Canadian taxpayers' money to be paid to anyone who is not a Canadian citizen in an industry which we consider so valuable and under threat from American interests is a matter which has to be addressed. I am obviously among many on this side of the House who will support this amendment when it is put to us. I hope the government will see fit to support it as well.
The hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture is conferring with a Saskatchewan member of Parliament at this moment. I am hoping that the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek has managed to convince the parliamentary secretary to change his mind. I certainly appreciate any efforts that Saskatchewan members from all sides of this House can make to ensure that this act is amended properly.

Motion No. 8
That Bill C-98 be amended in Clause 10 by striking out lines 3 to
9 at page 9 and substituting the following therefor:
"10. No information submitted by a producer for the purpose of administering a program established under an agreement may be communicated, disclosed or made available to an official of the Department of National Revenue without the prior written permission of the producer."

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
He said: Mr. Speaker, the existing legislation provides that information can be passed from the Department of Agriculture, the programs running GRIP and NISA, to the Department of National Revenue. We do not necessarily agree that even that should happen. Surely, if it is going to happen, there should be the permission of the producer.
I know every member of Parliament in this House has had the experience of making representations on behalf of constituents and has had to get a waiver so that they could make those representations. If a member of Parliament has to get a waiver from his constituent to make representations, to get a tax refund or to get a reassessment, it seems to me the Department of Agriculture should have to do the same.
Yet, this legislation gives you carte blanche. You just push the computer and you get a spit-out of it. That would be bad enough if it was a federal public servant who was doing it, but it is not even being administered by a federal public servant. If it were a federal public servant, we could come into the House and give his minister hell here on the floor of the House Commons.
This program is all going to be administered by provincial civil servants. How does a federal member of Parliament get after a provincial civil servant who abuses the income tax confidentiality rules? Surely it is reasonable that the government has to get permission.
We had quite a debate in the committee itself. I do not want to relate what happens at the committee because that is not protocol here, but essentially the government says: "Oh, well, we do this. When you sign the form you have got to get permission". That is fine. Why not have it in the statutes if at some future time some public servant or government decides that it is not going to get the permission of the producer to get this information from the Department of National Revenue, that it will just go ahead and get it, and that it is authorized by Bill C-98 so why bother?
This amendment is a very simple one. It requires that if the government is going to call up information-and this is generally speaking a crop insurance commission of the provincial government from the Department of National Revenue-then it has to get permission from the producer.
I have talked to many Liberal senators. They have told me that if this thing comes to them like this, then there is going to be great difficulty.
I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary, who is usually a very reasonable person although not always today, that if he really wants to expedite the passage of this bill and does not want to have it bounce back from the Senate, then he should accept this amendment.
It is reasonable. It is fair. It is in line with what the government is already doing. I do not know why the government should not be prepared to simply accept the amendment which says:
"10. No information submitted by a producer for the purpose of administering a program established under an agreement may be communicated, disclosed or made available to an official of the Department of National Revenue without the prior written permission of the producer."
It is a very reasonable, understandable clause. I was surprised at the incredible weakness of the parliamentary secretary's defence of the fact that the Government of Canada was going to provide a NISA account for non-residents and non-Canadian citizens.
To hear him tell it, NISA is like contributing to the western grain stabilization or receiving a benefit under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. For that matter, it is like getting the benefit which is implied when a producer delivers wheat to the Canadian Wheat Board and gets the initial price which may turn out to be higher than the market price.
NISA is a very special kind of deal. The producer can put in up 2 per cent of his qualifying income from his crop which is automatically matched by the government. He receives 3 per cent on top of commercial rates of interest which, right now, are probably 15 per cent. He can top it up with another 20 per cent of qualifying crop income. He will receive 3 per cent above the commercial rates of interest on that.
It is a very special arrangement. In this day and age of restraint, when we are cutting back on everything, we should not be passing this off as if it was the payment under ASA or under western grain stabilization. It is a very special arrangement. We are not proposing this kind
March 21, 1991

of arrangement for GRIP because it is a different kind of program.
The response of the minister was extremely weak on Motion No. 7. I would like to move Motion No. 8 which simply requires that the government gets permission from the producer whenever it is securing information from the Department of National Revenue.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this motion as well.
It is becoming very much of a communications world. The ability to move information and data from one place to another is becoming a great part of our life. Because of that, we are endangering, to a great extent, our privacy.
We have a tendency to say that we can trust Revenue Canada. If we have nothing to hide, Mr. Speaker, then we have nothing to worry about. However, that really is not the point.
The point is that what this clause gives in its present form is that:
Information submitted for the purposes of administering a program established under an agreement may be communicated, disclosed or made available to an official of the Department of National Revenue solely for the purposes of administering or enforcing the Income lax Act.
This assumes that the Department of National Revenue will ask for the agreement, but chances are it will ask for it on a broad basis and it will get a report from the program which will have listed everybody who has decided that he or she is going to be part of any of these programs.
Consequently, that is putting into the public domain information which we have always indicated in other programs is not available in the public domain.
As the former speaker suggested, even if we had a specific administrator whose responsibility it was to say yes or no to whether or not that information went to the Department of Revenue, that would limit it considerably.
But the real issue becomes whether any farmer who is part of this program wants this information to become part of the public record. The way it is worded at present, it can be. But I agree entirely with the position taken by the member for Algoma that agreements should be
Government Orders
confidential and it is up to the producer to decide what is and is not private information. If the government wants this information, it should come to the farmer for it. It should not be able to go some place else for it. In that case, the farmer has no control, or even any knowledge of what information is being given out concerning the business.
I think it is time we started taking a harder line on that kind of approach and this motion is a good start. In other words, if we are a democratic nation that puts a great deal of value in the individual and in the privacy of each one of us, then we must put safeguards into our legislation rather than leaving it open to any kind of meddling or information which can, not necessarily be harmful but which we do not necessarily want to be broadly known.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we can gain support for this particular motion. It is a very small change, it just goes from "information being available without any consideration to the participant", to saying that the participant must be at least informed. If he has nothing to hide, there is going to be no problem; if he does have something to hide, it is going to be a little more difficult to get it, I suppose. But that is still his right.

Mr. Speaker, this motion by my colleague from Algoma shows the diligence with which he has reviewed this bill. This is absolutely necessary. We have discussed this with members on the opposite side of the House and their quick answer is that this permission will be given on the application form.
But there is nothing in the legislation saying that that request for permission must be on the application form. I think in this country it is necessary and it is assumed that this type of permission be asked for.
This motion amending the bill serves the purpose of keeping the government honest, in making sure that it asks for that permission and does not go after this information without asking the private individual for permission to do so.
Again, I ask the government to reconsider. It is only common sense that the legislation say what the agreements do at present. This is necessary in order to make it legal and right and proper, so that the producers can have the protection they are entitled to in Canada.

March 21, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my two cents worth-three cents?
I think the amendment is utterly reasonable. The government, in effect, is saying to us: "You have our word. You have our promise that before any information is passed along to Revenue Canada, we will seek the permission of the producer. We will seek the permission of farmers". In fact, it is telling us that the forms already contain that provision. Well, I do not think that is good enough. When it comes to enacting good legislation, we should do it in a business-like way. Let us not leave anything to doubt.
I know the government says: "Our word is good. Do not worry, we are going to be honourable about this". If that is the case, I think it is quite reasonable to ask the government to go just one more step. Put it in the legislation. Put it there in black and white. Before anything like this is done, it will be put in legislation. It removes all doubt.
I hope that members opposite will realize what we are asking for and pass this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put forward a couple of thoughts relative to Motion No. 8. Certainly, one very similar had been dealt with in committee.
In any event, just before touching on that, there was some reference made to the previous Motion No. 7 by the member for Algoma and I am sure I will be allowed the same indulgence.
It is fairly evident that we have a long border between the United States and Canada, some 3,000 or 4,000 miles and that border is not one that is made out of stone, concrete or brick. It is not a Berlin wall, Mr. Speaker. It is one in which there are a number of natural occurrences such as rivers, streams and valleys. Along the length of a border like that, there would be people who farm, for no other reason than the terrain and the topography of the land on both sides of the border.
The understanding has always been that the rules apply equally to those people on both sides of the line. Therefore, it would seem inconsistent to exclude Americans or others, who farm on this side of the border from
participation in the Canadian programs when our people are accorded participation in like circumstances across the way.
The Western Grain Stabilization Act, I believe, was amended some time ago and among other things it allowed the privilege of participation to non-Canadians under these circumstances.
I think it was in that debate that the hon. member for Prince Albert at that time said, and I quote him, from the July 8, 1988 Hansard:
There is a concern that has been expressed about whether to extend this privilege of stabilization to non-Canadians. I know that that has to be dealt with within the Charter and it is something that we need to look at a little more closely, although I have no great concern about it myself.
He had no concern at all about extending stabilization to Americans a couple of years ago. It is hard to understand why there would be any concern today with the extension of that privilege of the farm income protection act benefits on a reciprocal basis.
Motion No. 8 is one which promotes a little bit of mischief, because if it was contained in the bill in the form which is proposed by the member for Algoma, it would, I believe, leave a false impression, an implication that a producer would have a choice as to whether to permit the exchange of information between Revenue Canada and the administrators of the program when in fact that is not the case at all.
With this wording, I believe that anyone reading it, such as a producer would assume that there was a choice involved. For that reason I have some concerns.
There are a couple of good reasons why the requirement is in the bill in clause 10 as written. I think the first is just a matter of audit purposes. There is a considerable amount of taxpayers' money going into these programs. It has always been the case that the taxpayers of this country expect prudent management of their money and they expect accountability. They would certainly expect that the program would be able to withstand audit. Then it becomes a question of the manner of enforcement.
At this point I would like to refer to the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1990 in which the Auditor General had quite a bit to say in regard to the Department of National Revenue, and in particular, about the economies that could be affected
March 21, 1991

through the use of computerization and through the use of matching. Indeed what he noted was among other things that most of the current matching process is highly automated and does not demand a great many human resources. He was saying that in the context of encouraging more use of computerization and more use of matching between sources of information in order to reduce the horrendous audit cost when you have people involved manually trying to track things down and to secure the information that they would require in the ordinary course, in the normal audit of any expenditure of taxpayers' money.
Again, the Auditor General mentions at page 566 of that report that the computer matching is highly productive and could be expanded:
Many new computer systems have been implemented in the last ten
years to improve taxpayer services, management information and
enforcement activities.
And so on. It indicates beyond any question and recommends that it would be wise for government in terms of economy to move toward more computerization and more matching and less reliance on person-years and the archaic and inefficient methods of the past.
Certainly, from the point of view of audit, which I think is inherent in any expenditure of taxpayers' money and there is a considerable amount of it here, it is not unreasonable to expect that if that is going to be done, and I think it has to be done, then it ought to be done in the most expeditious, most efficient way possible because I believe that all members of the House would want the administration of these programs done in the most effective and least costly way possible in order that the benefits can be paid out to producers rather than utilized in bureaucracy and that sort of thing.
The second point I want to make in regard to this is that I hope there is a potential, in regard to NISA, the Net Income Stabilization Account, that there could be some form of automatic triggering because one of the options is the taxable income. It might well be possible that there could be an automatic trigger through the exchange of information between the two programs.
It is quite clear that the information cannot be divulged in any event without the consent of the taxpayer or the program participant and the forms under the regulations have, as I understand it, that wording in

Mr. Speaker, I am quite amazed when I read the legislation and listen to some of the objections of the government members. Mr. Speaker, The Battlefords-Meadow Lake is one of those constituencies that is very much involved in agriculture. It is a constituency which rests a few miles north of Saskatoon and runs all the way up into the forest land of Saskatchewan. I have within my constituency some of the best farmland, the highest-yielding farmland, in the province and I run right through to some of the poorest farmland, the most marginal farmland, in the province. Therefore, I have some of the farming community that has been intensively involved in grains production and, without diversification, has been very hard hit by the changes in grain prices in the world market.
I also have those people who have had to all their lives carve out a little piece of land with a couple of cows, some chickens and hogs, and a small piece of grain land. Those people are the ones who are on the edge, who have no funds whatsoever to put into a NISA program. They have nothing in the bank; they are going from day to day. They are heavily in debt, making up a large percentage of the debt. They have not been involved in crop insurance or western grain stabilization. Therefore, any premiums that are going to be paid for a GRIP or NISA program are brand new expenses for a good part of the people who farm in the north-central part of my constituency.
For that cross-section of Saskatchewan producers, I am trying to speak fairly clearly to the government opposite which is putting together a program, an agreement, that is not on the table. The legislation that we are trying to deal with today that simply enables the government to create that agreement. The farmers of Saskatchewan, as are the farmers in the rest of Canada, are not in any position to debate or even think about the specifics in that agreement. There are crop insurance people in Saskatchewan right now going door to door talking to farmers, telling them that they had better sign up for this program because the premier of Saskatchewan has said that if they do not sign up for this program, they will not be eligible for any other program that comes out of Saskatchewan or out of the federal government.
March 21, 1991

These people who need cash to get their crop in the ground this year, who need to find a way to have their debt restructured so that they can survive until such time as there is adequate income produced from their industry, who are relying on us in this Chamber to provide for them an income protection and stabilization program that meets their needs have to be astounded by the way in which all of this process is happening.
I want to speak as loudly and as clearly as I can to the government opposite, to the parliamentary secretary, to the minister, to the Prime Minister, and say that these people need long-term income stabilization programs to secure their future in the industry and to secure the future of the industry in Canada: the agrifood industry, the agriculture industry, the farm industry. Without it, we are going to lose it.
Therefore, because all of this is involved in these agreements that are not on the table, we are stuck with having to amend bits and pieces of very flawed pieces of legislation in order to try to make the point to the government opposite that things are needed that are not there. Because this bill does not address the big picture, we are reduced to talking about little pieces of that big picture.
Therefore, I support the motion that is on the floor today from the member for Algoma. He has identified another small piece of this legislation that needs to be addressed.
I am concerned. If the government does not support this motion, which says that no information submitted by a producer for the purpose of administering a program established under agreement, may be communicated, disclosed or made available to an official of the Department of National Revenue without prior written permission of the producer, I am concerned about what it is behind its thinking. What is it trying to do if it will not allow the producer to be the one who controls the information that goes to Revenue Canada?
Many of my producers have had a great deal of difficulty with Revenue Canada over the last few years. Many of my producers live in that area that is marked for the northern tax allowance benefit program. Many of those people have been told one thing by Revenue
Government Orders
Canada one day, and the next day something else. It has ended up costing them $2,500 to $4,000 in the course of a year because of the way in which Revenue Canada has dealt with them. They do not trust Revenue Canada and they certainly do not trust this government in the way it is handling this type of situation.
I give a number of examples of this Revenue Canada activity. For example, when a producer signs on to the program and puts so much money into NISA, and has money matched by NISA and fills out the forms and does everything that needs to be done, that is not done for tax purposes. That is done for the business purposes of that farm operation. The piece of paper that has that information on it in the GRIP or the NISA program does not recognize that that producer may have that year been separated or divorced or lost a child or had a number of things happen within their family circumstances that has affected their income tax operation.
For this program to be able to transfer information about that farm operation from an agricultural agreement point of view, over to Revenue Canada, for Revenue Canada to interpret it, audit it, review it, do whatever Revenue Canada wants to, is a tremendous breach of the privacy and personal circumstances of those individual producers.
The information that is provided to the GRIP and NISA programs, when they are created and set up, have nothing to do with taxation matters. We fill out tax forms, we pay our taxes, we do what we are supposed to do. Revenue Canada has to accept those signed documents as being the documents that are, in essence, the documents for tax purposes. Not the GRIP and NISA agreements, not the GRIP and NISA forms, not the GRIP and NISA programs.
Therefore, I am very, very pleased with this amendment, as I have been with the amendments submitted by my colleague from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre here in addressing some of the things that have been missing from this legislation.
In the end, I would like to see the agreements come before this Parliament for full debate before they are accepted. I would like to see the future of agriculture as described by this government in terms of its programming for the next 50 years put in front of this Parliament for debate.

Growing Together, the paper that outlined in very general and nebulous terms what this government thinks it wants to do, has not been up for debate by this country and by this Parliament. We are very anxious to see some future for Canadian agriculture. Dealing with matters such as these, pieces of legislation that simply give the government carte blanche is something we do not want to do.
I appreciate the time and attention the members from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and Algoma have given to this bill, and to my colleague and friend, the member from Mackenzie, who has worked so hard for us in agriculture matters.
