Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a few comments to this motion if I could.
This motion is a good motion. It is motion No. 9 in the list of amendments. It has to do with clause 11 of the bill, which talks about a special measures committee.
A special measures committee is to review this bill where the minister is of the opinion that exceptional circumstances are important. In other words, where the third line of defence comes into place, there will be a committee that will be formed to advise the minister on what form a third line of defence should take.
The problem with clause 11, as was discussed many times during the committee debate, was that there are a lot of "mays" in this clause. It says:
That the minister may implement such procedures or other special measures as the minister considers necessary to determine the appropriate action to be taken to remedy those circumstances.
In other words, the third line of defence. It goes on to state:
That the minister may appoint a committee to be known as a special measures committee consisting of members who may -
This is the crucial word in this clause:
-who may represent Canada, may represent a province, may represent producers and may represent any group of persons who the minister considers appropriate.
In other words, the minister is to appoint a committee, but on that committee he can put anybody he wants. It
March 21, 1991

may represent Canada, the provinces, the producers. Of course, it may not represent them either.
The concern is that we should have a "shall" instead of a "may". Certainly, it would make people on this side of the House feel more comfortable, and I am sure it would make the producers across this country feel a little more comfortable if they know that the special measures committee shall consist of members who represent Canada, the provinces concerned, the producers and any other group.
What it does is solidify in legislation the fact that there will be a group formed that will be representative of producers; in fact, it will include them. We do not know what is going to happen down the road with this legislation. We do not know when third line defences will be required.
It is very important that we pass legislation that does not allow the government to get away with things. We do not know what type of government we will have in the future. We are sometimes surprised at the type of government we have had in the past. If we had a New Democratic government of course these matters would be different.
It is important regardless of which party is in power. All kidding aside, it is important whatever party is in power that there are some assurances, that the people of Canada have some assurances, that the producers of this country have some assurances that there is some protection for them in legislation.
What we are saying is that this is an important clause to be put in place. I am pleased that this matter was brought forth.
I want to make a couple of other remarks. This group, this committee that will be formed, is going to be a very important committee. The third line of defence is certainly an important factor in this whole bill. There is still much discussion to go on with respect to the third line of defence. As I said it will come from time to time. It is a worth-while committee which will be doing very important work. I am pleased that the government will see fit to let this motion pass.

Mr. Speaker, the motion I have placed before the House proposes two changes to the legislation as it now stands. The first, as does the previous motion, calls for an earlier review than is set out in the bill.
The bill calls for a review within the next five years and concern has been expressed by some producers, certainly producers from the prairie pools, that in fact there should be a review before that time, preferably starting within a year from now. We are dealing with new legislation that is going to have a lot of loopholes and problems. It is important that we tiy to get it right. In fact we look forward to a review process that is going to improve the program, that is going to provide farmers and producers across this country with a good program.
The second part of my motion deals with that review. The way the legislation reads now in clause 19, a review will simply be done by the minister and tabled in front of the House. Quite frankly, I have some concern with that in a couple of areas.
First of all, this is a bill that is dealing with hundreds of millions of dollars. This is an expensive program. This is also the first program coming out of the Growing Together paper. Hopefully there will be others, but this is the first piece of legislation. What we are doing is casting a new form; we are casting a new way for agriculture in this country. There is a new direction that is being set by this legislation.
It is very important as we set a new direction for agriculture that we ensure that there is a proper review process in place to fine-tune the legislation. This legislation needs some fine-tuning, but it is important that we
have a review process in place that is going to deal with the review and the necessary changes down the road.
The best place that can be done is through Parliament. We are all elected here to represent our various ridings and collectively the country. What has happened with Parliament over the years is that we have an executive that tends to dominate this place, especially with majority governments. We have a situation sometimes where we have a few members of the House who really dictate what goes through this House.
What we are talking about here is a fundamental matter involving the democracy of this nation. This motion does not call for the minister to do a review but for a committee of the House of Commons or the Standing Committee of Agriculture to do the review.
The government has indicated, and we raised this in committee, why do we have to have that? The committee of agriculture can review this any time it wants and so on. It is more important than that. Although the committee of agriculture can do the review, there is no guarantee in legislation that it will do the review.
We are seeing right now in this House all sorts of negotiations and problems happening with respect to the Standing Orders which are now in the process of being changed. In fact, the proposed set of Standing Orders that I saw are going to further limit the abilities of members of Parliament to carry out their duty. It is for that very reason that we need some kind of protection in legislation so that producers will know that in fact there is to be an all-party committee that is to have a good and thorough review of this bill.
There are precedents in this House for that. Most of them are relatively recent. I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the Employment Equity Act which in section 13 says that "five years after the coming into force of this act, and at the end of every three-year period thereafter, a comprehensive review of the provisions and operation of this act including the effect of those provisions shall be undertaken by such committee of the House of Commons as designated or established by the House for that purpose".
An act to amend the Parole Act and the Penitentiary Act says in section 14 that "three years after the coming into force of this act a comprehensive review of the provisions and operations of certain sections of this act shall be undertaken by such committee of the House of Commons or both Houses of Parliament as may be
March 21, 1991

designated or established by Parliament for that purpose".
The Privacy Act in subsection 75(1) says that "the administration of this act shall be reviewed on a permanent basis by such committee of the House of Commons, of the Senate or of both Houses of Parliament, as may be designated or established by Parliament for that purpose".
The Access to Information Act says as well, in section 75, that "the administration of this act shall be reviewed on a permanent basis by such committee of the House of Commons, of the Senate or of both Houses of Parliament, as may be designated or established by Parliament for that purpose".
The Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act, in section 56, also calls for a comprehensive review by a committee of the House of Commons that is designated or established by Parliament for that purpose.
The Official Languages Act in section 88 does the same thing.
There is a number of precedents and what these precedents do is establish in the legislation a permanent guarantee that this legislation will have a proper and thorough review by a committee of the House of Commons. We have seen it, as I said, with the proposed changes to the Standing Orders which are to limit further the power of members to carry out their function as members properly.
I have only been a member since 1988, but I have talked to members who have been here for a lot longer than myself. They are saying that they continue to see an erosion of their powers as individual members and that it is more difficult for them to carry out their duties. I find that one of the most satisfying aspects of being a member is working within committees. I find committee work is most rewarding. We have all-party committees so we have a view from all political perspectives. The committee is on an open basis. It gets together and decides what it is going to look at, who is going to be a witness in front of the committee, and sets out the task for that committee. It is gratifying, enjoyable and rewarding. We have to
Government Orders
be allowed to do our job. If the government continues to hamstring us then it is impossible to do that.
It is important to put this motion into the statute to guarantee to the producers in this country that there is going to be some thorough review, because this is a fundamental change in agriculture as we know it today. We are on the road to carving out a new direction. The government has talked, and I can say with some justification that there is consultation. There was consultation through part of this process.
After having looked at the legislation, farmers are now having some second thoughts on it. In front of our committee members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said: "We have to be careful. We are in a period of trusting the government to bring in decent legislation." They also said: "We have not really been consulted since August and we are hoping that the government will bring in proper legislation."
There have been comments like those and comments from other producers before the committee. Others who have appeared before the committee have said: "Look it, we are not really sure exactly which way the government is going with this legislation".
As committee members we have not seen any of the proposed agreements. They will not technically be signed until this bill is passed, but we have not seen the proposed agreements. We know snippets here and snippets there. We know what is going on in some areas, but we have not had a chance to look at this legislation. It is for that veiy reason that we should have in this legislation this clause that allows members of Parliament to carry out their duties properly so they can do a proper and thorough investigation of this bill at appropriate times, knowing full well that it will not be taken away at the whim of a majority government that wants to change the Standing Orders. It is for that reason that I do hope that the government and my colleagues in the Liberal Party will support this worth-while amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I guess it is a matter of either supreme confidence or supreme arrogance on the part of the government that it thinks that any legislation it can make is going to be perfect the first time out.
If we had a great deal of past experience that the legislation which has come out of this government can withstand the test of time, maybe we would say it was supreme confidence that would allow it to say: "We do

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
not need to look this legislation over for five years". However, we have many examples of poor legislation, legislation badly drafted and rushed through or pushed through without the right kind of vetting.
This particular legislation has within it a considerable amount of openness. On the surface that sounds like a good thing, but it is it is legislation which is allowing agreements to be established between the provinces and the federal government. It is giving a body outside the Parliament of Canada a considerable amount of power to spend taxpayers' money.
As I said, it may seem to be good legislation now but there is no guarantee. Possibly we might have even gone further than these two amendments and suggested that we have a continuous review of how this legislation is going to work. We could have suggested that we put on that review committee a number of producers from each of the provinces, from the administration of the plans and from the federal government.
This suggestion says: "Let us take a look at this as early as possible, in suitable times, and continue to look at it so that we have a fairly good control of how it develops".
As I said, if we could be confident that it was going to work and we had the experience that most pieces of legislation worked well, we would say: "Yes, go ahead. We will hold it for five years and then we will start looking at it". But we have to assume that it is not going to work. Many of the people who have looked at it closely are already saying that there are flaws in it which we are going to have to deal with as early as possible.
We are being told things almost daily by farmers who are becoming very knowledgeable about this legislation and about the agreements that this legislation allows. They are saying: "This is going to be good legislation for a couple of years, but what about that third year? There are certain things about this legislation that we already do not like. We should look at those right away of we should look at those at a very early stage".
If this legislation goes the way that some people expect it to go, it will go into huge deficits. Unless we have a consultation and review process in place which draws this Parliament back in, it is going to become a matter
between the two ministers of agriculture within the agreement they have signed. That is not the intent of the legislation. The intent of the legislation is to allow this Parliament to establish a structure for the agreements.
It is taxpayers' money we are putting on the line here, and a considerable amount of money it is. Therefore, it behoves us as responsible legislators to make sure that we protect not only the farmer in a different situation who can be gouged by this kind of legislation or these kinds of agreements, but also the taxpayer who foots the bill in the end if this becomes a costly runaway project.
Much as I want to have legislation that is going to help the farmer, I would much rather have stable legislation which makes the farmer look at it and say: "Yes, I can be part of this for the next ten years". If it is going wrong, I do not want him to leave. I want him to get in there and help fix it up. He must have enough confidence in it so that he would be part of the rearranging of the requirements which make it a good program. If we do not have the kind of review that is being suggested by these two motions, then we depend upon the minister.
There are three things about this review of which we should be careful. First, who shall do it? Second, how often should it be done? Third, to whom should it go, who should be involved in it and who should look at the monitoring of it? If we do that, we will have some kind of continuous monitoring of the situation and the parts of the legislation and the agreements which we already recognize as being flawed can be fixed up so that they will work.
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few short words.
Do you promise?

Yes, I promise. The main point of this motion is to draw attention to what could be a real problem with the way the bill is drafted now. As those of us who are watching the drafting of agreements between the provinces and the federal government are aware, those agreements are being signed for five-year periods. They come into effect on April 1 and they will lapse and be re-signed on April 1, 1996. It is extremely difficult to do a proper review, a serious review, if the review is
March 21, 1991

reported in at the same time as the new agreements are signed.
It is extremely important, if we are going to have a serious review, that it be done at least a year before those next agreements are signed, or the whole effort is futile. Therefore, I suggest that we pick one of these dates that are before us-they are only five or six months apart-and have the review done after a couple of years of experience. In that way, we will have some idea as parliamentarians, as farm groups, as provinces, and as federal negotiators, as to what pitfalls to be looking for well in advance of negotiating and signing the next set of agreements.
The way the legislation is currently, it has no chance of being a realistic review process if the review must be tabled for public discussion at the same time as the new agreements are being signed. The review will have no effect at all if those two dates coincide, because the public will not have a chance to take advantage of the studies and the evidence that was found during the course of the review. New agreements will be signed without the public or the farm groups being fully aware of the shortcomings of the previous arrangement.

Mr. Speaker, I also rise in support of the amendments introduced. What the amendment is asking for is that we put in this legislation a time for the review; one suggestion is 1992 and the other suggestion is 1993, with just a few months' difference between the two.
The essence, as my colleagues from Mackenzie and Moose Jaw-Lake Centre have pointed out, is the need to have this legislation reviewed not in the distant future but to have it reviewed a year from its coming into effect. As has been pointed out, this is a commitment of large sums of money.
Second, there are various and genuine concerns which have been expressed about this program. In the province of Saskatchewan, the provincial government has organized meetings across the province to tiy to explain GRIP and NISA. It has not been all that successful because it does not know the answers to the questions that the farmers are asking. There is a lot of uncertainty about this program. There is uncertainty about what the benefits will be. There is uncertainty about how much the fees will be. There is uncertainty about how it will work. Those who are out there to explain the legislation

cannot really answer the questions that farmers have been raising.
That is why the lukewarm reaction to the GRIP and NISA programs is not surprising. Many farmers are just backing off. In part, they are saying: we don't know enough about this. We are not prepared to commit ourselves and the sums of money that appear to be necessary to be able to enrol in the program. We are not prepared yet to commit that. That is another reason why this program should be reviewed.
It should be reviewed as well in one or two years time on the effectiveness of the program. Is it really doing what it is supposed to be doing? Is it creating the foundation for our farm economy, and is it doing it in an effective way? Or is it becoming a boondoggle?
There is a part of me that sniffs another scientific research tax credit scam here. It was a quickie little thing that the Liberals had introduced in the dying days of the government in 1984 and it resulted in the loss of several billions of dollars of money that was not properly used towards research and development. A lot of it was wasted, Mr. Speaker. Had that money been addressed to research and development then the state of research and development would have been in a much better position in Canada today than it is.
I have that same gnawing feeling here, that we are legislation that is so loose, its draftsmanship is so awkward, that it could result in the loss of large amounts of public money, most of which will not go to the people who need it the most. Most of that public money conceivably could go to a few individuals, while the vast majority of the farmers who need the money, those who are struggling to survive, who are being sucked under and down, are not the ones who will be receiving the type of benefits they will need in order to survive.
That is the fear I have about this program. I might be wrong. I hope I am wrong, I hope it does what the government claims it will do; that it will help family farms survive, and will allow a stable agricultural economy to flourish in Canada. I hope it does that. But let us make certain it does that.
Why not allow a review in 1992-93 to make certain that it does do that, to see if there is any need for some tinkering, for some amendments, for some adjustments? Every program needs adjustments. That is part of the

March 21, 1991
Government Orders
process of experiences; you experience things, you learn things, and you adjust as you go along.
Why does the Minister of Finance not do that? That is a whole other question about the Minister of Finance.
But what we are appealing for here in our amendment is for the government to recognize that it might need adjustments, and to allow those adjustments to be written into the legislation to ensure that this review will occur which involves all the farm organizations and the farm groups, that will involve Parliament and a committee of Parliament, the Standing Committee on Agriculture. These too should all be involved in the process of the review.
As members of this House, especially those who represent farm communities, we will pick up on how this program works and how it doesn't work. We will very quickly know the little idiosyncrasies in this program, the types of situations that even farm representatives, farm bureaucrats and even the minister in his office cannot even think of. We will pick up the little nuances and bring that experience and that information on to the floor of the House of Commons and into the committee on agriculture, so that our experience and the knowledge that we pick up in being members of Parliament are part of the input into this review process.
The amendment before us is a piece of common sense. I sincerely hope the government will be gracious in accepting the amendment because I believe it will strengthen the legislation. Hopefully it will create a bill, create a farm program that will do what I am sure all members of the House would like to see it do, enable a viable farm economy for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to comment on Motions Nos. 10 and 11. Between the two I assume that Motion No. 10 will come to a vote first. It seems to me that it is the preferable motion because it suggests that a review be made by April 1, 1993. GRIP really starts August 1, 1991. The terminal point for that crop year is August 1, 1992. The final pay-out comes some time after that, perhaps in the fall of 1992.
If we are going to have a reasonable review of at least one full year of the operation of GRIP, to try to do it before April 1, 1993 is simply not practical.
I would hope that if the government is accepting either one of these amendments that it would accept the first one standing in the name of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. It allows for one full year of operation of GRIP plus a few months afterwards so that we can at least have a report and a review which really reflects one complete crop year operation, taking into account premiums, the benefits paid out and the over-all operation to ensure that it is a reasonable and fair assessment of the value of the program.
I hope these comments will be taken into consideration by the government. We are very appreciative of the fact that Motion No. 5 has been accepted and does provide for some review, although it does not specify an exact date but provides for a continuing review without putting the deadline of April 1, 1993, as Motion No. 10 does.

Mr. Speaker, I have just three short points as the clock winds around to six o'clock. First, I want to thank the Minister of Agriculture for his presence in the House and take the opportunity to say to him that the farmers in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake and in Saskatchewan want to see some bridge financing now. They want to see some pay-outs in time for planting this spring. They are going to have to know about this now.
On behalf of the producers of Saskatchewan, of western Canada, in particular The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, I ask the Minister of Agriculture to make that pitch to cabinet and to make an announcement to the people on the prairies.
Don't tie it to GRIP and NISA.

As the hon. member for Regina-Qu'Ap-pelle indicates, don't tie it to GRIP and NISA. I think that is very important too. Do not say: "Sign up or you don't get this". That is a very important point. The finance is necessary now. We know GRIP and NISA is coming later.
The second point is also on a congratulatory note. I notice in Bill C-98 a clause concerning environmental assessment. This is the first time I have noticed an environmental assessment written into government legislation. I think this is a major step forward in the legislative process. I want to encourage the government
March 21, 1991

to continue to do this in all of its legislative processes, as well as all of its policy making. I have a couple of problems with the way in which it is written into the bill, but I am pleased to see that the step has been taken. The fact that we could have environmental assessment after the damage has been done by the bill is a matter that concerns me.
The third item I want to raise is this amendment. I support the motion in front of us, because I believe a review of the bill within the timeframe set out in the amendment is much more important than the timeframe set out in the bill itself.
The points that were made by the hon. member for Mackenzie are very well taken, that in fact this review must take place before any renegotiation, any new signing of any agreement occurs. The review process is very important.
As my friend from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre pointed out, it is very important we ensure that the review process is conducted by parliamentarians who have regular day to day discussions, communications, consultation with the producers who are the people who put us into this place to speak on their behalf in matters such as this.
With those few points, I hope the amendments that were put forward here today by members of the opposition will be supported by the government. I wish us all well in the deliberations that come and on our speeches at third reading, whenever that takes place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one theme that has come up repeatedly in the past few federal budgets is that Canada is facing a huge deficit. Too large a percentage of Canadians' tax dollars is going to paying the interest on the deficit. If moves are not made to decrease the deficit immediately, then the burden on future generations will be unmanageable.
I am sure we are all in agreement about the seriousness of the deficit and that reducing it is important. However, what we do not agree on is how best to reduce it.
Perhaps I can just make an analogy to describe what I see as the present government's method of reducing the
deficit. Suppose a homeowner had a leaky roof but no money to repair it. Surely, it would be wise to find the money somehow in order to repair that roof. By not repairing the roof, in time it will fall and the homeowner will have no place to live. In addition, the loss of a substantial investment will take place.
Unfortunately, it is clear that the government and its economic policies follow an approach which is permitting the roof to fall in. It is not investing in the future.
We have seen cutbacks to social programs of all kinds that would have been inconceivable 10 years ago. Many feel that programs that make us proud to be Canadians, such as medicare, will soon be lost with the lessening of federal contributions to the provinces.
Colleges and universities are being forced to raise tuition fees because with less support from the federal government, this is the only way that they feel they can raise money to ensure continued programs.
The result is increasing inaccessibility of post-secondary education with more and more less well-off Canadians being turned away from an education. All these cutbacks are in the name of reducing the deficit. All Canadians must do their part is what we have been told by the government.
Are all these cutbacks really going to help reduce the deficit in the long run? I fear that by cutting back on social programs, we are allowing the roof to slowly cave in. The price we will have to pay to fix it in the future will be very great, indeed.
A Senate committee which looked at child poverty recently heard a report estimating that children who drop out from school due to poverty over the next 20 years will cost the economy $33 billion. That is an amount greater than this year's entire deficit.
Are poor families getting any help from the government in this budget? Clearly, they are not. On top of the blow of the GST, we are seeing further limits to cap funding, cuts to transfer payments to the provinces and still no national child care strategy.
There are no spending measures intended to combat the effects of the recession. Unemployment premiums will rise and the benefits from unemployment insurance have decreased. This is not good news, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you will agree, for the 10.2 per cent of Canadians who are unemployed.

All these cuts I have just mentioned will certainly have an impact on poor Canadian families and on their children. Children are poor because their parents are poor. I think that, all too often, this government ignores this fact.
When we hear about 1.4 million Canadians being out of work, that is not just 1.4 million Canadians who are suffering. It is many more than that in terms of families with children who are finding it difficult to provide basic food, shelter and clothing for themselves.
That is 1.4 million families with children who are at risk of dropping out of school because of poverty. That is happening at a cost of $33 billion to the economy over 20 years as predicted before the Senate committee.
Is this the kind of social financial planning that will reduce the deficit, cut spending here and there to save now with the result being huge expenditures down the road to pay for those, by comparison, relatively small cuts now? I do not think so.
Perhaps I could provide another example: the case of low birth weight babies. Annually, Canada has spent over $200 million a year caring for low birth weight babies. All these costs do not end just with the initial care. Low birth-weight babies are at high risk of infant mortality, many illnesses, intellectual language and motor disabilities, increased rates of school failure and are at high risk of being socially maladaptive.
Would it not be wise to provide poor pregnant women with adequate food and nutrition before the baby is born? The cost would be marginal in comparison to the huge financial and human costs incurred after they are born. I do not think anybody could argue that this would not be a wise investment. Yet the government continues to ignore these problems in Canada, sending the message to poorer Canadians that they must do their part to help fight the deficit.
The fact of the matter is that if the government only invested in poor families now, the poor would be able to do more than their fair share to help fight the deficit later. They would help save the government many times over what it is saving by cutting social programs.
Adjournment Debate
I am past appealing to members of the present government on the basis of their compassion, their compassion for poor children who are ridiculed at school because they wear clothes from the Salvation Army, and who cannot stay awake in school because they have not had anything to eat for breakfast. I am past the point of asking for compassion for the single mother who works eight hours a day for minimum wage.
I am trying to appeal to the only thing that the government seems to understand or care about and that is the bottom line. To invest today in Canadians is a good investment; it will save billions of dollars in the future. The alternative, which is presently being followed, is to save a relatively small amount of money now, with the result being a generation of Canadian children being sacrificed to poverty, only to incur greater expenses in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the hon. member's question and attempt to explain government spending and transfer payments to the provinces. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does not seem to understand how the federal system of transfer payments to the provinces works. The two main ways the government transfers sums of money to the provinces are what we call established programs financing and equalization payments.
Mr. Speaker, established programs financing is money that is apportioned equally to all provinces on a per capita basis. Equalization consists in payments made to the so-called poorer provinces. Most provinces receive both transfer and equalization payments. This includes Quebec and a number of other provinces.
The provinces are given this money to spend as they see fit. This year, over $36 billion will be transferred by the federal government to the provinces, who will use this money to finance education, hospitals, and all other areas under their jurisdiction. Mr. Speaker, federal transfers to the provinces were not cut in the latest Budget because this year-if I compare with next year and two years from now-the provinces will receive more money than they received last year. There was a reduction in the increase, and I am sure the hon. member will understand when I explain this in terms of his salary. His salary hasn't been cut, but the increase to

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to address an issue of major importance for Canadians generally, but more specifically for those in the Montreal area.
On December 10 last, I directed a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration concerning the tragic job situation in the Province of Quebec. At the time, Quebec had lost 87,000 jobs over the previous six months and I had predicted that the situation would deteriorate even further. Mr. Speaker, I was right.
As recently as three months ago, I asked the Minister to take concrete measures to create long-term jobs as well as implement immediate programs to assist working men and women who had just lost their jobs.
In her reply at the time, the Minister of Employment and Immigration stated that employment programs were available in Quebec and that these programs would bring results which would meet my expectations.
I must say today that, as far as job creation is concerned, I am not at all satisfied with the results this Tory government's initiatives have brought to the Montreal area.
And the basis of the information I have received from Statistics Canada, I must conclude that the programs to which the Minister alluded to, last December, were nothing but empty shells.
Mr. Speaker, let us have a look at the results the Conservatives have obtained with their job creation initiatives. Today, one out of every four Montrealers lives under the poverty line. The unemployment rate on the territory which includes the Island of Montreal and Island of Laval reached 15.1 per cent in February, according to Statistics Canada. Of all the major Canadian centres, Montreal had the highest unemployment rate. Some 225,000 Montrealers are unemployed.
Such is the result brought about by this government's employment policies. Although the unemployment rate in the Montreal area keeps increasing, we are still without any economy recovery program to create longterm jobs.
On top of this economic flight we now have to contend with the last Tory budget. This Budget, tabled on Februaiy 26, is not providing any assistance program to the unemployed. Quite the contrary, Mr. Speaker: The Minister of Finance announced in his Budget speech a $100 million cut from its Canadian Jobs Strategy.
Another factor which is hardly conducive to job creation is the research and development funding reduction. As evidence of this, total 1987 federal government expenditures for that item amounted to 1.4 per cent of the gross national product, as compared to only 1.28 per cent now.
Mr. Speaker, I am asking the Minister of Employment how does she expect Canadians to believe that this government is serious when it affirms that it wants to create permanent jobs and help the unemployed when in fact all the basic job creation programs are reduced?
Then again, Mr. Speaker, bankruptcy figures contribute precious little to restore the confidence of the unemployed looking for work. In excess of 11,000 companies went belly up in 1990, and this figure has been on the increase ever since. The result of these bankruptcies is a direct increase in unemployment levels. I have already pointed out that Montreal's unemployment rate now stands at 15.1 per cent. Unemployed Montrealers are not in a mood to rejoice when they see these figures.
Quebec is not immune to the havoc stemming from the bankruptcy trend. The number of Quebec bankruptcies soared to 40 per cent in the first months of 1991. Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada officials tell us that 1,618 individuals have sought protection under the Bankruptcy Act. Yet the minister told me on December 10 that I would be pleased at the outcome of job creation programs.
March 21, 1991

Who can possibly rejoice over a 40 per cent rise in the number of bankruptcies? Mr. Speaker, who can possibly rejoice over an unemployment rate topping 15 per cent?
I can assure the Minister of Employment and Immigration that nobody is pleased in Montreal. Would the minister care to ask the 1,800 General Motors employees who have just been told they will be laid off for one year whether they are going to be pleased?
I spoke about the economic situation in Montreal on a number of occasions since December 10, and again yesterday, Mr. Speaker, and I am still waiting for concrete measures designed to boost the economy in the region of Montreal.
So again I ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration what measures does her government intend to take to create jobs in Montreal before it is too late? What does the government have to offer to the 225,000 people who are out of work in the region of Montreal? Mr. Speaker, let us hope again that she has more than pious wished to express.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 7, 1990,1 rose in this Chamber to ask a question about the northern tax allowance, a matter which is very important to a large number of residents in my constituency in northwest Saskatchewan.
My question was not adequately answered by the Minister of Finance at that time, and subsequently he has announced that a new permanent program will be established to replace the current one, the one that we found most unfair and discriminating.
However, during the past year, and for some during the past 18 months, residents of my constituency have been left in the dark about how the old tax program and now the new one would be applied in their area. For one part of my constituency the question is still not resolved, and for another the resolution of the question is totally inadequate. I am still trying to get this government to acknowledge that a fundamental unfairness is affecting the residents of the towns of Loon Lake, Makwa, and the rural municipalities of Loon Lake and Beaver River.

March 21, 1991
Adjournment Debate
I have contacted the finance minister and the minister responsible for Revenue Canada on numerous occasions, and they are well aware that the people in these communities and rural municipalities were once declared eligible for the northern tax benefit in 1987 but were then subsequently reviewed and disqualified and forced to pay back taxes for which they had been eligible under the program. They were asked to pay back taxes with fines, interest and penalties, including court costs for some who took the matter to tax court and some now in the Federal Court of Canada.
There are two bits of unfairness in all of this. First, the people of these areas were told one thing and then assessed differently and penalized for it. Second, they remain as isolated and northern as any of the other residents in the surrounding areas who are eligible for the northern tax benefit.
Let us take the village of Pierceland, for example, which is inside the boundaries of the rural municipality of Beaver River. By a special order, the people of Pierceland are eligible for the northern tax benefits but the rural residents who may live 50 feet outside the town's boundaries are not eligible.
A nurse at the hospital who lives in town will get the benefit; the nurse who lives out of town does not. There is no fairness in that program.
Another example is a teacher who lives in the town of Loon Lake but works in the town of Meadow Lake, a half hour drive away. That teacher who lives in Loon Lake does not get the northern tax benefit, but the teacher who may live across the street from the school in Meadow Lake does get the benefit. That is not fair.
I might add that the new program established by the minister does not correct the unfairness of this. I want to ask the minister to put Loon Lake, Makwa, the rural municipality of Loon Lake, and the rural municipality of Beaver River on par with the program for the towns of Meadow Lake, Pierceland and Goodsoil.
I also want to ask the Minister of Finance to re-evaluate the new program to ensure that there is justice within it. For most residents in my constituency currently eligible for the benefit, the benefit program will be phased out by the 1995 tax year under the new program.
All of these people presently benefiting from the tax program should not be disentitled by 1995. They are northern and isolated by definition. If they are considered to be in need of this tax break today, I see no reason why they should be considered less in need in the future when they are asked to be phased out of the program.
As I see it, all Canadians should pay tax and for the taxes we pay we must receive a service. For the residents of southern and urban Canada the direct government benefits for their taxes paid are accessible. For those who live in Ottawa for example the services of government are more accessible than for those who live outside of Ottawa. For those who live in southern and urban Saskatchewan, the benefits of government are much more accessible than the benefits available to those who live in northern and isolated communities.
But every resident of Canada pays tax and theoretically it is an equal portion of tax. For northern residents, the benefits are not as accessible as for those in the southern part of the program. The northern tax benefit, as I understand it, simply recognizes that northern residents do not have equal access to government programs and returns to them some of their tax dollars in compensation for that lack of access.
Otherwise, our unfair tax program is even more unfair with northern and rural people paying a greater share than is warranted. I am hoping the Minister of Finance can correct this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the northern tax allowance program, which came into effect in 1987, every person who has been living in an eligible community for at least 6 months is entitled to the maximum $450 monthly deduction. Furthermore, the employee and his family are entitled to a deduction for travelling expenses paid up by the employer, including up to two trips a year for vacation purposes, as well as any travel taken for medical reasons.
Under the 1987 program, determination of eligible communities created some administrative problems because the criteria were applied on a local basis. It was time-consuming and led to mistakes. Problems surfaced because certain communities were eligible while neighbouring towns were not. This had to be replaced.
March 21, 1991

To this end, the Minister of Finance established, on April 29, 1988, the Task Force on Tax Benefits for Northern and Isolated Areas. Its mandate was to look into the eligibility criteria and to make recommanda-tions for improving the program. The task force submitted its report to the minister on October 27, 1989.
The task force members took 18 months to study the question and prepare their report. They held consultations across Canada and made a thorough analysis of the subject. The task force concluded that a zonal approach was the most equitable and simple solution. Since the task force report was submitted to him, the Minister of Finance has received hundreds of letters and documents on this issue and has consulted with the communities concerned on many occasions.
Following these consultations and the review of the task force recommandations, the minister has developed a new northern tax allowance system for Northern and isolated areas. According to this new system, the inhabit-
Adjoumment Debate
ants of the northern area, as recommended by the task force, will be entitled to the entire deduction, up to $450 per month, while people living in an intermediate area will receive half of the benefits provided. Moreover, residents of communities for which the benefits will be reduced or removed will have a long transitional period.
This new program meets adequately the general consensus on the need to reform the old program which provided disparate benefits. It will allow for elimination inequities, facilitation of compliance with the rules and improvement of the administrative process. It will also provide more efficient tax assistance to residents of remote areas of the North.
